class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez ? Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Bringing calm, hope back </h3><p>Little Village, the predominantly Mexican American Southwest Side neighborhood, was <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2026/02/20/operation-midway-blitz-effects-latino-neighborhoods-pilsen-little-village-southeast-side" target="_blank" ><u>at the center </u></a>of immigration enforcement operations last fall. Whirring helicopters and whistles warning that immigration agents were near became the norm.</p><p>Vero Ortiz, senior director of community wellness for the not-for-profit organization Enlace Chicago in Little Village, remembers it this way: “There were days that you wouldn’t see anybody on the streets. There was just so much fear. And now we’re living in the underbelly of that fear.”</p><p>While fewer agents roam the streets and enforcement has become more targeted, Ortiz says the psychological impact persists.</p><p>Ortiz lives in the suburbs and has worked for Enlace for two years but identifies as someone “adopted by Little Village.” As a first-generation Mexican American, Ortiz speaks to having a strong cultural connection to the neighborhood, which is why having to fight a system Ortiz says is trying to erase the vibrant community has prompted grief, anger and stress.</p><p>“I cried this morning,” Ortiz says. “I saw a post of a little girl standing between an ICE agent and her mom, right? It’s still happening.”</p><p>Ortiz’s powerful emotions, however, have not hindered their work. Rather, they fuel it, with a drive to offer more preventative options to help residents be empowered and ready for the next crisis.</p><p>Ortiz has been working to meet the surge in need for mental health services. They secured city funding this year for an additional community-based therapist and a school-based therapist as well as for a new family support specialist who could help, for instance, people who might still be afraid to leave their homes. <i> </i></p><p>“We can sometimes work at 100 miles an hour even though, as leaders, we’re not asking our staff to do it,” says Ortiz, who has worked in child welfare and gang intervention. “I think they do it because they love what they do. So it’s also my responsibility to be, like, ‘Hey, I’m going to need you to not burn yourself out’ because I need my staff to be well in order for us to serve the community.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Feixu Chen</i></p><p><i>Mary Ellen Ritter and Navya Shukla produced this story as part of the Medill Investigative Lab-Chicago at Northwestern University.</i></p><p><i>This story was produced as part of the</i><a class="Link" href="https://mentalhealthjournalism.org/parity-collaborative/" target="_blank" ><i> <u>Mental Health Parity Collaborative</u></i></a><i>, a group of newsrooms and universities covering mental health care access and inequities in the United States.</i><br></p>

entries.title: How does Chicago’s cultural spending compare to other cities?
entries.summary: <p>New York City’s buzzy progressive mayor, Zohran Mamdani, took to social media last month to announce — <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/16/nyregion/mamdani-mandarin-video.html?unlocked_article_code=1.6FA.y-v3.m0wB9a7x4XGy&smid=nytcore-ios-share" target="_blank" ><u>in multiple languages</u></a> — an initiative to give thousands of free Broadway tickets to local high school students.</p><p>Paired with a recent, <a class="Link" href="https://www.artforum.com/news/mamdani-allocates-a-record-323-million-for-culture-1234753986/" target="_blank" ><u>record-setting $323.8 million</u></a> allocated for New York’s Department of Cultural Affairs in the city’s budget, Mamdani appears intent on building a reputation as a culture-forward mayor. His enthusiasm comes as <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2025/05/03/nx-s1-5385888/sweeping-cuts-hit-nea-after-trump-administration-calls-to-eliminate-the-agency" target="_blank" ><u>federal arts support</u></a> has withered under President Donald Trump, and as private foundations that buttress the arts shift their priorities elsewhere. That’s made local government investment more critical than ever.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" data-align-center> <div id="Form-newsletter-wrapper" class="Form-newsletter-wrapper" strong support. Now, three years into Mayor Brandon Johnson’s term, as the city heads into its fall budget season and gears up for a mayoral election, WBEZ/Sun-Times asked advocates and the mayor himself about the city’s commitment to the arts and crunched the numbers to look at how Chicago’s budget stacks up compared to other major cities.</p><p>Across the country’s five largest cities (New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston and Phoenix), Chicago was the only one to cut the funding for its local arts agency during its most recent budget cycle. And while its spending dwarfs that of the larger Los Angeles, and trails only behind New York in per capita arts dollars, the pressure is mounting on city leaders to do more.</p><p>“I don't like to compare myself to any other place because there's just no comparison to the cultural, the art scene in Chicago,” Johnson said in an interview last week about arts under his leadership. “What I can say, though, is for me, making the investments in arts and culture, that I believe is the way to define my administration.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-8b0000" name="html-embed-module-8b0000"></a><div style="min-height:697px" id="datawrapper-vis-45p9T"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/45p9T/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-45p9T"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/45p9T/full.png" alt="Chicago shrank its cultural affairs budget this year, while other big cities raised theirs (Bar Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>In 2026, Chicago allocated about $22.70 per capita to the city’s arts department, trailing behind only New York (which spends $37.72 per capita). But the Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events, known as DCASE, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/city-hall/2025/11/05/chicago-dcase-cultural-affairs-budget-clinee-hedspeth-kenya-merritt-grants-arts" target="_blank" ><u>took a 15% cut</u></a> in the 2026 budget.</p><p>“I think local governments really need to get creative about funding the arts and to really look at new, interesting, dynamic ways to figure out how to increase those resources,” said <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2025/05/23/erin-harkey-dcase-trump-arts-funding-nea" target="_blank" ><u>Erin Harkey</u></a>, Chicago’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/culture-the-arts/2024/03/04/chicago-dcase-leadership-in-flux-after-erin-harkey-termination" target="_blank" ><u>former cultural czar</u></a> who now leads the national advocacy group Americans for the Arts.</p><p>And as the city gears up for another <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2026/08/25/mayor-brandon-johnson-refinance-debt-city-hall-budget-deficit" target="_blank" ><u>tough budget fight this fall</u></a>, with some cultural organizations <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/classical-music/2026/05/07/chicago-sinfonietta-layoff-program-pause-finance-classical-music-2027" target="_blank" ><u>gasping for air</u></a> or <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/dance/2025/04/17/chicago-links-hall-dance-closing-small-venue-financial-trouble-arts" target="_blank" ><u>shutting down entirely,</u></a> some arts leaders and advocates worry about what comes next.</p><p>“When the arts and the cultural community contributes to the city in such meaningful and obvious ways, that should also be reflected in the budget,” said Meg Leary, a local artist who recently launched <a class="Link" href="https://www.artsfirstfund.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Arts First</u></a>, a new collective arts fund intended to give dollars directly to artists.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-960000" name="image-960000"></a> The creative sector is actually Chicago’s third-largest industry, accounting for nearly 213,000 jobs, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2026/06/25/creative-economy-impact-study-arts-alliance-illinois-workers" target="_blank" ><u>a 2026 report</u></a> by Arts Alliance Illinois.</p><p>Cultural attractions such as the city’s restaurant scene and outdoor music festivals are <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/mayor/press_room/press_releases/2025/october/summer-tourism-records.html" target="_blank" ><u>tourism generators,</u></a> cites <a class="Link" href="https://www.choosechicago.com/press-media/press-releases/chicago-welcomes-56-8-million-tourists-in-2025-generating-a-record-breaking-21-5-billion-in-spending/" target="_blank" ><u>Choose Chicago</u></a>. The resuscitation of the zombie-like Loop post-COVID? The <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/economy/2025/10/15/chicago-loop-foot-traffic-post-pandemic-arts-culture-events" target="_blank" ><u>arts get much credit</u></a> for that, too.</p><p>Plus, cities with stable support for the arts saw their local creative sectors emerge stronger after the blow dealt by the pandemic, according to <a class="Link" href="https://culturaldata.org/media/3245/cityartssectortrends_fullreport.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>a new national report</u></a> from SMU DataArts in Dallas.</p><p>“Nobody, as an arts worker, is getting up because they’re, like, ‘I’ve got to contribute to the GDP’ or ‘I want to stimulate economic activity on this corridor,’ but these are real facts,” Harkey said. “And if something is this massive and this important to the economy, we have to pay attention to it.”</p><p>Each major city approaches its local arts agency slightly differently: Chicago’s includes the “special events” arm that programs everything from Taste of Chicago to Blues Fest; New York allocates money for city-owned spaces like the Metropolitan Museum of Art; and Houston has a designated external nonprofit partner to distribute grant dollars. In Chicago, DCASE’s funding comes primarily from the city’s special events and hotel tax, plus a mix of public and private grants.</p><p>As New York’s cultural affairs budget increased by 8.1%, local arts funding also climbed in the most recent budget cycles in Phoenix (by 2.3%) and Los Angeles (by 4.7%). In Chicago, funding trended downward in the 2026 budget.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-ff0000" name="html-embed-module-ff0000"></a><div style="min-height:428px" id="datawrapper-vis-GFWHU"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/GFWHU/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-GFWHU"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/GFWHU/full.png" alt="Selected cities’ average spending per resident on cultural affairs departments (Column Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Still, Johnson — who has not confirmed if he will <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/city-hall/2026/08/27/chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-august-ask-the-mayor-live-questions-call-phone-number" target="_blank" ><u>seek reelection</u></a> next spring — said he is committed to investing in the sector. In Illinois, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2026/02/23/pritzker-budget-arts-funding-flat-illinois-2026-2027-grants-trump" target="_blank" ><u>funding for the arts</u></a> remained mostly steady under Gov. JB Pritzker’s most recent budget.</p><p>Still, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2025/11/13/nora-daley-richard-m-daley-chicago-arts-culture-architecture-biennial" target="_blank" ><u>Nora Daley</u></a>, board chair of the Illinois Arts Council, said that budget item does not reflect the full picture of what the state spends on the sector.</p><p>“It's a very tough budget time in Illinois, especially with all these federal cuts, so I think we have to look at new models and partnerships,” Daley said.</p><p>When it comes to sourcing further investments in the arts, Johnson pointed again to his trademark theme of progressive revenue — that is, taxing corporations and high-income individuals at a higher level.</p><p>“My preference is always that we're investing more,” Johnson said. “We'll continue to do whatever we can to ensure that the city of Chicago remains at the cutting edge when it comes to not just investments but shaping culture.”</p>

entries.title: Joffrey Ballet President and CEO Greg Cameron to step down in 2027 after helping steer financial turnaround
entries.summary: <p>Joffrey Ballet President and CEO Greg Cameron will step down in December 2027, marking a 15-year tenure that brought more financial stability, the company announced Thursday.</p><p>A board search committee will select a national firm to find Cameron’s replacement, who is expected to start before the end of 2027.</p><p>Cameron, 68, said his succession plan has been in the works for three years, and that he is neither retiring nor moving on to lead another organization. But he plans to stay connected in the Chicago arts community while pursuing other interests.</p><p>“I’m energized,” he told the Sun-Times. “It’s time for me to make room for the next generation of leaders. I've worked in the cultural space in Chicago for 44 years, and over my tenure, I've seen people stay at the party too long. I didn't want to stay at the party too long.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-260000" </figure> </div> </div><p>Since joining the Joffrey in 2013, Cameron has brought financial stability to the organization, eliminating a budget deficit and establishing its first-ever endowment, which has grown to<b> </b>approximately $30 million. During his tenure, the operating budget more than doubled from $13 million to about $33 million.<b> </b>In 2025, the Joffrey <a class="Link" href="https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/364009741" target="_blank" ><u>reported nearly $40 million in revenue</u></a>, making it one of the top-earning arts organizations in the city.</p><p>Cameron is also credited with strengthening Joffrey's international reputation. He oversaw the company’s move from The Auditorium to the Lyric Opera, which has allowed for more ambitious productions, including the critically praised “Frankenstein,” in 2023 and crowdpleaser “Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland” last year. The company opens its 2026-2027 season on Sept. 17 with “Liliom,” which features the choreography of Milwaukee-born dancemaker John Neumeier, the longtime principal choreographer of the Hamburg Ballet.</p><p>Cameron also facilitated partnerships with leading ballet companies on programs, including several with roots in literature, such as “Anna Karenina” with The Australian Ballet, “Princess and the Pea” with Oregon Ballet Theatre, “Atonement” with Ballett Zürich and “Eugene Onegin” with San Francisco Ballet.</p><p>Cameron said the Joffrey was already on a positive artistic trajectory when he started, but he and then-board chair Zachary Lazar determined financial challenges.</p><p>“We had moments of peeling back an onion and discovering, ’This isn't working,’” Cameron said. “We developed specific plans and righted the ship.”</p><p>Part of that strategy was getting the board more engaged in thinking beyond minimum contributions of their “time, talent and treasure,” Cameron said.</p><p>“In my life, success has never been tied to thinking about the minimum,” he said. “If our dancers came into the studio and thought, ‘What's the minimum I can do?,’ we wouldn't be having the success artistically at the box office. it comes to programming, Cameron said he is most proud of growing the “Winning Works” competition, which provides emerging choreographers with opportunities to create new works with dancers from the ballet’s Grainger Academy. Cameron also supported the creation of a documentary about the initiative, “<a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/about/about-pbs/blogs/news/joffrey-ballet-the-next-movement-introduces-five-rising-choreographers-helping-to-redefine-ballet/" target="_blank" ><u>Joffrey Ballet: The Next Movement</u></a>,” directed by Cam Be and produced by Kartemquin Films. It premieres Sept. 18 on PBS.</p><p>Joffrey Artistic Director Ashley Wheater said Cameron’s leadership has allowed him to achieve his creative goals, staging reimagined versions of everything from “The Nutcracker” to “Of Mice and Men.”</p><p>“Greg has really made my dreams become a reality,” Wheater said. “I think it has definitely put the company in a very unique place within America, in that we have a very unique repertoire. You can dream big, but if you can't support those dreams, they're not going to happen.”</p><p>That support included clearing the Joffrey’s debt, unifying the various administration departments and establishing critical partnerships with the Lyric Opera, Chicago Symphony Orchestra and other institutions, Wheater said.</p><p>“He is such a part of the cultural fabric of Chicago,” Wheater said. “And he's charismatic. He knew exactly the right people to talk to in order to get things done. People that had never really been involved with the Joffrey suddenly became very involved. class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Cameron strengthened the company’s international reputation by facilitating partnerships with leading ballet companies on programs, including “Eugene Onegin” with San Francisco Ballet this year. Victoria Jaiani, who played the female lead of Tatiana in the production, posed for a portrait in a rehearsal room at the Joffrey Ballet on May 26, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Arthur Maiorella/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Cameron’s other accomplishments include guiding the ballet through the COVID-19 pandemic, establishing the “Joffrey for All” commitment to accessibility and expanding dance education in Chicago Public Schools. He also supported ongoing union efforts, negotiating two five-year contracts with the American Guild of Musical Artists. He said he hopes to solidify a third five-year agreement this fall.</p><p>Under his leadership, the Joffrey has also partnered with other cultural institutions on a plan to revitalize Downtown with a so-called “<a class="Link" href="https://www.culturalstadium.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Cultural Stadium</u></a>” concept that would pair events and architectural features. Among those projects is Poetry Way, an activation of the alley between Joffrey Tower and the Chicago Theatre, which will launch on Oct. 17 during the Chicago Loop Alliance Arts Fest.</p><p>“I am part of a team that has accomplished all of this,” he said of his overall success at the Joffrey. “I am not the artistic director. I can't dance. I don't sing. I don't paint. I don't draw.”</p><p>Despite that, Cameron has had a passion for the arts since he was a child in Westchester. He even created a makeshift museum in his basement, charging neighborhood kids to see his grandparents’ tchotchkes from their travels around the world, as well as his pet boa constrictor. Then, he graduated to hosting theater productions<b>.</b></p><p>“I was not performing,” he said. “I was printing the tickets, advertising and closing the garage door between acts.”</p><div entries.title: Are cicadas louder this year?
entries.summary: <p>From Garfield Park to Lake View, from Oak Park to Belmont-Cragin, cicadas are singing their summer chorus across the Chicago area.</p><h3>Cicadas make a racket every summer. But is the cacophony of buzzing, whirring and droning louder this year?</h3><p>It’s “inconclusive” whether they’re louder, said Spencer Campbell, the Morton Arboretum's senior manager of natural areas. Anecdotally, Campbell said, cicadas seem louder this year, which could have something to do with a very hot summer in the Chicago area. But some studies have shown that cicadas are actually less active in warm weather, he noted.</p><p>People may be more attuned to the insects because in 2024, Illinois was the epicenter of a once-in-a-lifetime <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cicadas" ><u>convergence of cicadas</u></a> that emerge every 13 and 17 years.</p><p>There may also be more of them than usual. Nina Salem, founder of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/06/05/insect-asylum-aims-to-inspire-with-public-cicada-art-now-on-display-cicada-parade-a" >Insect Asylum</a> in Avondale, has noticed more cicadas compared with last year.<b></b></p><p>Two weeks ago in Palmer Square, cicada nymphs were crawling out of the ground and climbing onto Salem like a tree. “I can’t remember the last time in the city that cicadas were emerging underneath me and crawling up,” she said.</p><p>“We definitely have more luck in finding them than before,” said Salem, who opened the Insect Asylum’s museum in 2022. “We’ve had a really cool cicada season.”</p><p>Cicadas do seem louder this year, observed Salem, though she noted that’s based on her personal experience, not science.</p><p>She wondered if more-forested areas like Thatcher Woods, LaBagh Woods and Skokie Lagoons are seeing — and hearing — more cicadas.</p><h3>Why do cicadas buzz so loudly?</h3><p>Males are sounding off ardent mating calls to attract females. They can climb high into trees “trying to yell louder than their neighbor,” said Campbell. Cicada choruses can exceed nine decibels — a noise level similar to that of lawnmowers, motorcycles and tractors. “Areas with more mature trees could have a louder chorus,” he said.</p><h3>What kind of cicadas are these?</h3><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/cicada-watch-2024/2024/05/24/periodical-cicadas-sound-buzzing-chicago-illinois" ><u>trademark end-of-summer buzzing</u></a> is coming from “dog-day” cicadas. They are annual cicadas, which is a misnomer since they can emerge every year or every two to five years, said Campbell. They come out only for a few weeks in the summer to mate before dying off. Their peak time is now. “A month from now this will be a distant memory,” he said.</p><p>Annual cicadas usually sing at dusk. Periodical cicadas that emerge every few years or more are loudest in the late morning and early afternoon.</p><h3>Are these cicadas part of the 2024 convergence?</h3><p>No. In 2024, for the first time in more than 200 years, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/outdoors/2024/03/14/cicadas-2024-illinois-map-schedule" >two types of periodical cicadas came above ground at the same time</a>. One brood, or breeding group, emerges every 13 years, and the other comes every 17 years.</p><p>In 1803, the last time that natural phenomenon took place, “electricity hadn’t been invented, horses and carriages were still the main way to get around, and the Great Chicago Fire hadn’t yet ravaged the city,” wrote Sun-Times reporter <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/mary-norkol" ><u>Mary Norkol</u></a> in 2024. Norkol has written extensively about cicadas.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-190000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A periodical cicada flies away from Stephanie Adams, plant healthcare leader at the Morton Arboretum, Friday, May 17, 2024. The periodical cicadas have emerged in the Chicago area for the first time in 17 years.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Scientists and researchers, like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/outdoors/2024/03/14/cicadas-2024-illinois-map-schedule" target="_blank" ><u>Kacie Athey</u></a> of the University of Illinois, encouraged people to appreciate that rare occurrence.</p><p>“We talk about this as being a once-in-a-lifetime thing where two are coming out at once, it’s more than that. … The next time we can expect to see two broods to come up is 2245,” Athey said then.</p><p>When the cicadas emerged from their years feeding underground, one <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/6/3/23747337/chicago-outdoors-here-come-the-cicadas" ><u>brood that emerges every 17 years</u></a> was centered in northern Illinois, while the 13-year brood was found in the southern part of the state.</p><p>Although the 2024 event captured headlines, this year’s annual emergence is “exciting,” said Salem of the Insect Asylum. She noted that the general public doesn’t celebrate more common events as much.</p><h3>How are people coping with cicada noise?</h3><p>Even if this year’s cicada ruckus is at normal levels, some people on social media describe their droning as “deafening.”</p><p>At Keshet, a private therapeutic day school in Northbrook, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/cicada-watch-2024/2024/05/06/cicadas-autism-sensory-sensibilities" >students with disabilities and sensory sensitivities again prepared for cicada noise</a> and changes in their environment.</p><p>“Many of Keshet’s programs are located in Chicago’s northern suburbs, and the cicadas have been really, really loud this summer,” Jennifer Phillips, president and CEO of Keshet, said in an email. “Our staff continue to be aware of how the noise can affect individuals differently and provide support and accommodations as needed.”</p><p>Students, ranging in age from 12 to 15, go over <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2017/12/6/18375402/blue-mind-why-being-near-the-water-makes-you-happy" ><u>coping mechanisms</u></a> if the cicada noise becomes overwhelming, such as going inside to take breaks from the noise, putting on headphones or chewing on a toy to help distract themselves.</p>

entries.title: Every known federal prosecution in Chicago tied to Trump’s immigration blitz
entries.summary: <p>Federal prosecutors in Chicago have accused 33 known defendants of nonimmigration crimes tied to Operation Midway Blitz. Many were accused of assaulting or resisting federal agents or officers.</p><p>Two defendants have pleaded guilty. Twenty-five have been cleared. Grand jurors refused to indict at least three of the 25, and another member of that group was found not guilty at trial.</p><p>One of the 25 saw their charges dropped through a deferred-prosecution agreement. Under the terms of such a deal, prosecutors agree to drop charges if a defendant abides by certain terms over a set period of time. Six Midway Blitz defendants struck such a deal, and five are still pending.</p><p>The Chicago Sun-Times is tracking all of the known criminal cases tied to Operation Midway Blitz:</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-6e0000" name="html-embed-module-6e0000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-table" data-src="visualisation/27349648"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/27349648/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="table visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><div class="PageListO" data-module data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-bb0000" name="list-bb0000"></a> <div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> Latest from Jon Seidel </div> </div> </div> <div class="PageListO-items"> <div class="PageListO-items-row"> <div class="PageListO-items-column" data-with-borders> <div class="PageListO-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bearing-the-blitz/2026/09/02/federal-judge-told-things-are-no-longer-quiet-as-midway-blitz-lawsuit-faces-critical-november-ruling" >Federal judge told 'things are no longer quiet' as Midway Blitz lawsuit faces critical November ruling</a> </div> <div class="PageListO-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/02/broadview-six-luis-uribe-customs-border-protection" >'Broadview 6' scandal won't derail trial of CBP agent accused of 'gunpoint sexual assaults'</a> </div> <div class="PageListO-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/31/loretto-hospital-anosh-ahmed-broadview" >Indicted ex-Loretto Hospital exec primed to point to feds' wrongdoing if he can't cut a deal</a> </div> </div> </div> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: 2 more belugas die at Shedd Aquarium
entries.summary: <p>Two beluga whales died at the Shedd Aquarium on Wednesday, the institution announced.</p><p>One whale, a 20-year-old female named Rain, had been rescued weeks earlier from shuttered Canadian aquatic park where dozens of now-rescued whales were living under allegedly poor conditions. The other, 34-year-old Beethoven, was part of Shedd’s resident beluga pod.</p><p>It's unclear if their deaths were related, the Shedd said in a statement released Thursday morning, about a week after another rescued beluga, Peekachu, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/08/26/one-of-the-shedds-rescued-beluga-whales-has-died" >also died of unknown reasons</a>.</p><p>"These losses are hard, made more difficult by the fact that it will take time to get concrete answers about what led to their passings," the Shedd said in the statement.</p><p>The aquarium said it will perform tests to learn more about why they died.</p><p>"Some answers may come quickly, while others may take more time to come into focus. Given how closely the public has followed the rescue effort, Shedd felt it was important to share this news now rather than wait for every answer," the statement reads.</p><p>The Shedd said it was necessary to help rescue some of the 30 belugas that were struggling in the Marineland Canada aquatic park in Niagara Falls, Ontario. </p><p>In total, the Shedd was expected to rescue 10 belugas, adding to the eight that had already been living at the aquarium.</p><p>The Marineland park closed to the public in 2024. Marineland officials, citing extreme financial difficulties, had threatened to euthanize the whales if permanent homes couldn’t be found. For years, the park faced criticism that its animals were living in unsanitary conditions.</p><p>The Candian belugas "had nowhere else to go," the Shedd said in its statement. "Shedd and accredited partners were asked to step in. Helping these animals in need is part of Shedd’s responsibility, and our commitment to these whales and their second chance remains unchanged. We appreciate the outpouring of support from so many others who are equally committed to animal welfare.</p><p>"Shedd will continue to closely monitor, evaluate and care for the entire beluga population around the clock in the days and weeks that follow," the statement concluded.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/08/12/shedd-aquarium-to-receive-four-more-beluga-whales-from-marineland" >Shedd Aquarium to receive four more beluga whales from Marineland</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/07/22/belugas-chicago-shedd-aquarium-marineland-canada-rescue" target="_blank" >Rescued belugas have arrived in Chicago. The move is unprecedented — and controversial</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/animals/2026/07/23/first-look-belugas-shedd-aquarium-whales-canada-trip" target="_blank" >First look at Shedd Aquarium’s newest beluga whales: Acadia, Lillooet, Osiris, Sierra</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/08/26/one-of-the-shedds-rescued-beluga-whales-has-died" >One of the Shedd’s rescued beluga whales has died</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: What is Ye’s legacy in Chicago?
entries.summary: <p>Even though Kanye West was born in Atlanta, it was Chicago where he grew up and<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/making/2023/05/04/making-kanye" target="_blank" ><u> found his voice.</u></a> Here he went from handing out mix tapes on the South and West sides, to cutting his teeth as an uncredited producer, to releasing chart-topping singles and headlining major shows.</p><p>But West, who has changed his name to Ye, has become a polarizing figure in recent years. After taking out an<a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/jan/26/kanye-west-takes-out-full-page-ad-apologising-for-antisemitic-behaviour-and-denying-he-is-a-nazi-ye" target="_blank" ><u> ad in the “Wall Street Journal”</u></a> apologizing for antisemitic and racist behavior, he has set off on a redemption tour with two nights of stops in Chicago.</p><p>Ahead of this week’s nearly sold-out Soldier Field performances, WBEZ/Chicago Sun-Times asked<b> </b>four Black Chicago writers to reflect on the legacy of Ye (formerly Kanye West) in the city that helped entries.title: I’m a Chicago rabbi, and I choose to forgive Kanye
entries.summary: <p>What does mental illness look like in the Black community?</p><p>Sometimes, it's the unhoused guy on the CTA Red Line threatening to decapitate someone before the train gets to Roosevelt Road.</p><p>Sometimes, it’s the guy walking through your alley with his two Rottweilers, pulling his shopping cart with the rooster in the child seat.</p><p>Alternatively, it can look like a billionaire musical icon whose impact reached an entire generation — not only Black youth, but people everywhere.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-850000" name="module-850000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><b>Ye’s Chicago legacy</b></h3>Ahead of this week’s nearly sold-out Soldier Field performances, WBEZ/Chicago Sun-Times asked four Black Chicagoans to reflect on the legacy of Ye (formerly Kanye West) in the city that helped shape him.<br><br>Arionne Nettles on <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2026/09/02/ye-kanye-west-chicago-legacy-cultural-influence" target="_blank" ><u>the legacy of the ‘Old Kanye.’</u></a><br>Nile Lansana on <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2026/09/02/ye-kanye-west-legacy-touch-the-sky-love-eroded" target="_blank" ><u>how his bulletproof love for Kanye has eroded</u></a><br>Mary L. Datcher on <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2026/09/02/ye-kanye-west-chicago-history-legacy-dr-donda-west" target="_blank" ><u>why there’s still from at Chicago’s table for Ye</u></a></div> </div><p>I loved Kanye. There was a time I was so proud he could be the gift my city gave to the rest of the world. His work was equal parts musical brilliance and evocative snapshots of South Side coming-of-age experiences. It captured familiar places and adventures, content that resonated deeply with many of us who grew up in this city. He was us, and we were once him.</p><p>Then he suffered the unthinkable. He lost his mom, who had been his anchor and, at times, his muse. The one person more proud of him and who he was becoming than anyone else could ever be. Speaking as a mother, I don’t think she wanted to take a piece of him with her. That's not how we love. We want to leave a piece of us with them so they never forget what true love feels like, especially in a world where compassion and vulnerability are seen as weaknesses.</p><p>I've seen up close the torment children can suffer when they lose their mothers. But the people I know had the privilege of falling apart and starting the lifelong process of rebuilding themselves in private – away from cameras, tabloids, record labels and fans. They didn't have to be everything to everyone when they themselves felt tiny under the boulder called grief.</p><p>I believe this was Kanye. This loss would have been enough to cause mental distress in many of us. He forgot how truly grand he was and the amount of influence he still had. By losing a mother his influence couldn't save, he forgot his power.</p><p>I believe that's why he said hurtful things, such as how “slavery sounds like a choice,” or talked about how much he hated Jews. He forgot how powerful he truly was. But no one else did. That's why there were Black kids calling themselves Hitler and doodling swastikas in class, when many of them could barely spell their own names.</p><p>I also believe it was the reason he never invited the kids he once recognized wanted “to rap and make dope beats, just like you” or like him, on his record label.</p><p>He knew them. Once, he was with them. He knew about the record industry. He knew about the predators who’d only give record deals to young artists willing to promote murder music, the killing of their families and neighbors, that more often than not led to their very own demise. I know. I've been to some of the funerals. He could've helped stop the carnage and given so many of these boys a chance to grow into men, but he forgot that he was powerful enough to do it. Or strong enough to save anyone else if he couldn't even save the person he loved most.</p><p>I don't hate Kanye. Especially in this season, when Jews forgive and ask for forgiveness. It’s the time where we pray for redemption. I don’t believe any of us are beyond that. Not even Kanye.</p><p>I have watched his outbursts in horror at times, just like the rest of us. And as a Jew from the South Side, I chose to forgive him and to still find ways to love him. He has plenty of people constantly reminding him of all of the problematic things he’s said and done. I choose not to be a part of that.</p><p>I love him because he loves my city as much as I do. I just want him to remember his true purpose. I want him to be the entertainer that may have left, but now realizes how important it is for him — and us — to come back home.</p><p><i>Rabbi Tamar Manasseh is a speaker, activist and the founder of the antiviolence nonprofit Mothers and Men Against Senseless Killings. </i></p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydqyuid-l-i/" target="_blank" >Mom of Faceworld gang member found guilty of retaliating against a witness in son’s murder case</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydqyuid-l-d/" target="_blank" >Frank Main</a></h5><p><b>Mom's alleged role</b>: Donnita Bryant wasn't accused of pulling a trigger, taking part in a kidnapping or committing any of the other brutal crimes federal prosecutors have tied to the South Side street gang known as Faceworld. But prosecutors say the mother of a convicted Faceworld killer joined her son's campaign of intimidation — and helped post a videotaped law enforcement interview on social media to brand a government witness a "rat."</p><p><b>The conviction</b>: On Wednesday, a jury found Bryant and a Faceworld associate guilty of conspiring with her son to retaliate against witnesses in his murder case — the latest development in a sprawling FBI crackdown that's swept up at least a dozen reputed Faceworld members over the past three years.</p><p><b>Son's plea</b>: Earlier this year, Bryant's son Diontae Harper pleaded guilty to a federal charge that accused him of firing into a car at a South Side gas station and killing a 22-year-old man in 2020. He also pleaded guilty on Aug. 17 to the charges in the witness retaliation case.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The case offered a window into the violence prosecutors say Faceworld unleashed on West Chatham and surrounding South Side neighborhoods — more than a dozen killings, the gang rape of a woman forced to drink bleach and Harper's behind-bars campaign to expose government witnesses. The Faceworld investigation was part of a broader federal effort to rein in violence linked to Chicago gangs like Goonie Boss, Hobos and O Block.</p><p><a class="Link" Will it be enough?</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydqyuid-l-o/" target="_blank" >Brett Chase</a></h5><p><b>Keeping the lights on</b>: ComEd customers have footed the bill for billions of dollars spent by the utility in recent years to help ensure that power stays on in Northern Illinois even during the worst weather. ComEd says it needs to raise more than $15 billion through rate increases to handle rising demand and intense storms that experts say are getting worse because of climate change.</p><p><b>Is that enough?</b> The lights still went out in 2.4 million homes during storms this year. Sometimes, it was for an hour or less. People in the south suburbs have been left without electricity for as long as five days. ComEd said the number of outages citywide this year would be twice as high had it not made technological improvements in recent years to better deal with weather-related damage.</p><p><b>At issue</b>: The utility and state officials say more must be done to strengthen parts of the grid that are many decades old, in addition to the $4.4 billion already being spent on a previously approved initiative to strengthen the electric grid.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydqyuid-l-b/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>MORE IN ENVIRONMENT ⚡</h4><div target="_blank" >Selena Fragassi</a></h5><p>There's only one way to sum up the eclectic range of acts appearing at the Sound & Gravity Festival this weekend, a lineup that includes electro rockers Son Lux, ambient master Grouper and avant-jazz ensemble Natural Information Society.</p><p>"The band has either played at Constellation or should have," said festival creator Mike Reed.</p><p>The boutique venue, 3111 N. Western Ave., is where Reed books a mix of modern jazz, contemporary classical and experimental acts year-round. And it's one of the seven concert halls participating in the multiday, multivenue festival that returns Sept. 3-6 to the Avondale area for its second year.</p><p>Programming the festival in one centralized area of venues (where Reed also lives) is twofold. First, he said, "I wanted to get away from the festival of 20,000 people in the park, which I think has in a lot of ways played itself out, at least in Chicago."</p><p>But the other reason was to encourage music fans to easily jump from one venue to the next and discover a new band — or a new neighborhood. Sound & Gravity's website offers a map with eight different restaurants to check out nearby, too, like Indian street food eatery Thattu and BBQ hot spot Soul & Smoke.</p><p>"The core of our audience is people who are interested in discovery," said Reed.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydqyuid-l-tu/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What's something in Chicago that, despite its name being changed years ago, you still find yourself calling it something else?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). entries.title: Extreme heat continues in Chicago area Thursday ahead of cold front, rain
entries.summary: <p>Weather officials issued an extreme heat warning on Thursday for the Chicago area, marking the third day of dangerously high temperatures.</p><p>Before the warning expires at 7 p.m., temperatures could feel as hot as 101 degrees due to high humidity, according to the National Weather Service.</p><p>Sunny skies and an actual high of 94 degrees are expected to give way in the afternoon to a cold front and 40% chance of showers and thunderstorms, when temperatures are expected to drop, according to weather service.</p><p>This is the third consecutive day of heat-related warnings from the National Weather Service.</p><p>The Chicago area was placed under heat advisories on Tuesday and Wednesday. Temperatures peaked at 95 degrees on Tuesday and 96 degrees on Wednesday at O'Hare Airport, according to the weather service.</p><p>The heat index peaked at 106 degrees on Monday at Midway Airport, according to the weather service.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7a0000" entries.title: Bystanders caught in crossfire include woman killed, man wounded in Lockport Township
entries.summary: <p>Two bystanders, a woman who was fatally shot and a man who was wounded, were caught in crossfire while standing outside a home Tuesday night in Lockport Township.</p><p>Will County sheriff's deputies were called about 7:55 p.m. to the 200 block of Dellwood Avenue in Lockport Township in reference to a shooting call, according to a statement from the sheriff's office. </p><p>Deputies arrived on scene and found the two victims in a driveway, a 31-year-old woman and an adult male. Both were rushed to a nearby hospital, where the woman was pronounced dead and the male is expected to recover, according to the statement. </p><p>Preliminary investigation shows the victims were merely bystanders who got caught in some sort of crossfire while they were standing outside, </p><p>This remains an ongoing investigation and victim’s identity will be released by the Will County Coroner’s office. See less<br></p>

entries.title: Woman critically injured in Bronzeville shooting
entries.summary:
Police are looking for the assailant who opened fire at a 33-year-old woman, critically injuring her Thursday morning in Bronzeville.

At about 7:50 a.m. the woman was outside in the 4000 block of South Lake Park Avenue when a black car approached her and a gunman exited and opened fire in her direction, hitting her in the chest and arm, police said.

The attacker jumped back in the black car and sped away north and the woman was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center in critical condition, police said.

No arrests or other injuries were reported

Area 1 detectives are investigating.

entries.title: ‘Las cosas no están tranquilas’: demanda contra el Operativo Midway Blitz enfrenta una decisión crucial en noviembre
entries.summary: <p>La jueza que una vez desafió al comandante de la Patrulla Fronteriza, Gregory Bovino, y trató de limitar el uso de la fuerza por parte de los agentes federales durante el Operativo Midway Blitz ahora se espera que decida a mediados de noviembre si permitirá que la demanda de Illinois y de Chicago sobre la campaña de deportaciones prosiga.</p><p>La jueza federal Sara Ellis dictará su fallo el 17 de noviembre sobre el intento del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) de que la demanda sea desestimada. Fijó la fecha tras escuchar 3½ horas de argumentos el miércoles en la misma sala donde en otra ocasión ordenó a Bovino que compareciera.</p><p>Los argumentos se presentaron cuando Chicago estaba a punto de conmemorar el primer aniversario del Operativo Midway Blitz. Comenzó el 8 de septiembre de 2025, y resultó en ocho semanas de caos, gas lacrimógeno y miedo. Los federales dicen que la campaña terminó a fines de 2025, pero los abogados de Illinois claramente no están convencidos de que haya concluido.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d40000" name="module-d40000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>De hecho, los abogados acusaron recientemente a los federales de reanudar el uso de munición química, arrestos sin orden judicial y operativos de aplicación de la ley cerca de lugares sensibles como cortes. La corte de inmigración de Chicago lideró al país en audiencias en junio.</p><p>“Las cosas no están tranquilas”, dijo el abogado de Illinois, Vikas Didwania, en un escrito presentado ante la corte la semana pasada.</p><p>La demanda alega que la administración de Trump “desató un bombardeo organizado contra el Estado de Illinois y la Ciudad de Chicago” diseñado para “coaccionarlos” para que abandonaran las políticas de santuario, que implican que las autoridades locales no colaboran en la búsqueda de inmigrantes sin estatus legal.</p><p>Entre otras cosas, pide a Ellis que bloquee intentos futuros similares de aplicación de la ley de inmigración por parte del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional y de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza (ICE).</p><p>Ellis, nombrada a la corte por el presidente Barack Obama en 2013, se hizo cargo del caso tras tramitar litigios similares el otoño pasado. Había dictado una medida cautelar preliminar el 6 de noviembre que limitaba el uso de la fuerza por parte de los federales durante la campaña, leyendo el poema "Chicago" de Carl Sandburg mientras fallaba.</p><p>La Corte de Apelaciones del Séptimo Circuito bloqueó y luego anuló su orden.</p><p>La audiencia del miércoles en el nuevo caso giró en gran parte en torno a argumentos técnicos legales, incluida la cuestión de si Illinois y Chicago tienen derecho a demandar. Pero Ellis y los abogados exploraron las diferencias entre la campaña de 2025 y la aplicación de la ley de inmigración, ahora más agresiva aunque más silenciosa.</p><p>La jueza también reflexionó sobre un esfuerzo por hacer cumplir una de sus órdenes el otoño pasado.</p><p>Ellis lo planteó mientras les pedía a los abogados que identificaran la línea entre una aplicación legítima de la ley de inmigración y el tipo de coacción que alegan Illinois y Chicago. Quiso saber, "¿En qué momento... me salgo de mi carril?"</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" </div><p>Eso es porque, antes de dictar su medida cautelar el otoño pasado, Ellis había emitido una orden de restricción temporal similar. Luego, a finales de octubre, ordenó a Bovino que compareciera en su sala para discutir si esa orden se estaba cumpliendo. El exfuncionario de la Patrulla Fronteriza se había convertido en la cara pública de Midway Blitz, y desde entonces se ha jubilado.</p><p>“Había emitido una orden válida que decía, ‘Esto es lo que se puede usar, esta es la cantidad de fuerza que es apropiada en este entorno particular’”, dijo Ellis el miércoles, “y ciertamente era mi impresión que esa orden no se estaba cumpliendo, ¿verdad?”.</p><p>La jueza intentó entonces obligar a Bovino a regresar regularmente a su sala durante el transcurso de una semana. Explicó el miércoles que había querido retroceder con él sobre eventos que ya habían ocurrido. Si le hubiera pedido que le dijera qué iba a hacer al día siguiente, dijo, eso habría equivalido a que ella gestionara indebidamente el poder ejecutivo.</p><p>Pero terminó habiendo “una diferencia de opinión sobre si eso violaba la separación de poderes” entre las cortes y el poder ejecutivo, dijo.</p><p>La corte federal de apelaciones determinó que sí.</p><p>“Creo que esto ilustra muy bien lo complejo que puede ser”, dijo Ellis a los abogados el miércoles.</p><p>El abogado del Departamento de Justicia, Brantley Mayers, argumentó que Illinois y Chicago quieren quedarse con lo mejor de ambos mundos: no quieren apoyar el esfuerzo migratorio federal, y tampoco quieren que los federales desplieguen más recursos para hacerlo por su cuenta.</p><p>Pero Ellis le dijo, “No creo que eso sea lo que están argumentando, para nada”.</p><p>“De lo que se quejan, en este momento, es de que hubo una serie de arrestos sin orden judicial”, dijo Ellis. “Que la gente era detenida en la calle. Que la gente era detenida al dejar a sus hijos en la escuela. Que la gente era detenida al ir a la iglesia. Al ir al supermercado. Que personas que vivían en un complejo de apartamentos vieron agentes descendiendo por el costado de su edificio en plena noche y entrando.</p><p>“Que ese tipo de comportamiento, combinado con el trato a las personas que protestaban por el aumento de controles migratorios... cruzó la línea entre la aplicación y la coacción”.</p><p>Lee Reeves, coabogado de Mayers, le dijo a la jueza que la demanda había sido interpuesta por los demandantes equivocados presentando las reclamaciones equivocadas. Afirmó que las personas que creen haber sido perjudicadas durante la campaña deberían presentar demandas individuales o denuncias penales, en su lugar.</p><p>Varios individuos han hecho exactamente eso. Muchos han pedido que los agentes federales enfrenten cargos penales por supuestas malas conductas durante Midway Blitz.</p><p>Mientras tanto, el abogado de Illinois, Paul Berks, invitó a los federales a plantear otra afirmación: que la demanda está "sin objeto". En otras palabras, que no hay razón para preocuparse de que Midway Blitz vuelva a ocurrir.</p><p>Reeves y Mayers no aceptaron la sugerencia.</p><p>“Nos encantaría ver la evidencia de que no va a volver a ocurrir”, dijo Berks.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Here's what to expect while traveling over Labor Day weekend
entries.summary: <p>Travelers hitting the skies and roads over the upcoming Labor Day weekend can expect busier airports and highways — and to face higher prices.</p><p>The cost of airfare and gasoline is up this year. And airports are projected to be packed over the historically busy travel period.</p><p>About 1.71 million travelers will pass through O'Hare and Midway airports from Thursday to Tuesday, according to the airline projections shared by the Chicago Department of Aviation. That's 5.9% more passengers than the same period last year.</p><p>The busiest day at O'Hare should be Sunday, when 261,000 passengers are expected to pass through. Monday will be the most crowded day at Midway, with nearly 58,000 travelers.</p><p>Nationally, the U.S. Transportation Security Administration projects air travel to be nearly as busy as 2025's Labor Day weekend. Last year's holiday weekend was <a class="Link" href="https://www.tsa.gov/news/press/releases/2025/09/03/tsa-screens-record-104-million-individuals-over-labor-day-weekend" target="_blank" >historic</a> for the TSA, when it screened the most people every in a single day (10.4 million on that Friday.)</p><p>Meanwhile, the price of an average flight is <a class="Link" href="https://newsroom.acg.aaa.com/aaa-labor-day-travelers-face-higher-costs-and-heavier-traffic-wi/#" target="_blank" >up 2%</a> over last year, averaging $750 for a round trip ticket, according to auto group AAA. Ticket prices are up 20% to the most popular Labor Day destinations, such as Seattle, Orlando and Boston. The cost of international flights, however, is down 4% on average.</p><p>Travelers' pocket books are being pinched elsewhere. The cost of hotel bookings is also up 9% compared to last year, according to AAA. </p><h3>Car travel</h3><p>The cost of driving is up, too, as gas prices remain high than last year. The national average for gas was $4.14 a gallon on Wednesday, up nearly a dollar from last year's Labor Day weekend, when the national average was $3.19.</p><p>Vehicle traffic is expected to be worst in the afternoon and early evenings of Thursday and Friday as holiday travelers share the road with commuters, according to transportation data company INRIX.</p><p>The Illinois Tollway expects 8.5 million vehicles to use the toll system over the holiday weekend. The busiest travel days are projected to be Friday, with 2 million drivers, and on Tuesday, with 1.8 million drivers. The tollway typically sees an average of 1.7 million users each day.</p>

entries.title: Chicago Jazz Festival 2026
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson and the Chicago Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events (DCASE) are proud to welcome back the<b> Chicago Jazz Festival</b>, presented by Wells Fargo, taking place Thursday, Sept. 3, through Sunday, Sept. 6, at Millennium Park. The beloved Labor Day weekend tradition returns with four days of <b>free performances</b> featuring internationally acclaimed artists, and celebrated Chicago musicians.</p><p>Don’t miss headliners like Grammy-winner Dee Dee Bridgewater, jazz innovator Robert Glasper, the Miles Electric Band celebrating the Miles Davis Centennial, and Paquito D’Rivera. Plus, experience local legends, special tributes, and the WDCB Jazz Lounge—all for free, all weekend long. For the full lineup and details, visit ChicagoJazzFestival.us.</p>

entries.title: Felon who posed as Pablo Escobar's son admits bilking pro basketball player and others out of millions
entries.summary: <p>He was Pablo Escobar’s pretend son.</p><p>But the millions he stole from investors were very real.</p><p>Jawad Fakroune, a Chicago businessman, was already serving a federal sentence of six and a half years for terrorizing a restaurant owner. Now he has agreed to plead guilty to a fraud scheme that fleeced investors of millions while he dodged federal and Illinois taxes.</p><p>Fakroune admitted bilking at least $5.7 million from more than a dozen people, including an unnamed professional basketball player who handed him roughly $2.45 million in 2022.</p><p>Fakroune promised him that he would put the money into a shipping-container business and California marijuana-growing operation. Instead, Fakroune blew much of it on himself, according to his plea deal.</p><p>The money helped pay for Fakroune's residential compound in Lemont, rent on a New York City apartment, restaurant tabs, shopping sprees at designer stores, luxury watches and a 2022 Cadillac Escalade he bought for another person, according to the plea agreement.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div hustle.</p><p>Another investor, identified as “Individual L,” turned over approximately $2.85 million to invest in Fakroune’s phony cannabis business. She was promised a whopping 30% return after just three months.</p><p>To make the scam look legitimate, Fakroune showed the investor marijuana packaging he claimed came from the grow operation and staged phone calls with supposed investors, according to the plea agreement. Last year, Individual L lied to FBI and IRS agents about her dealings with Fakroune, authorities said.</p><p>Under his plea agreement, filed Wednesday in federal court in Chicago, Fakroune admitted to wire fraud and tax evasion. He agreed to repay his victims more than $5.7 million, along with back taxes.</p><p>If U.S. District Judge Thomas Durkin approves the deal, Fakroune would get an additional prison term of at least 12 months and no more than 42 months to be served on top of his existing extortion sentence.</p><p>In January, a federal jury convicted Fakroune of violently trying to collect $1.5 million from his restaurant business partner, Adolfo Garcia. Secret FBI recordings captured Fakroune threatening to kill Garcia and his family, and a hidden camera showed Fakroune assaulting Garcia at a River North restaurant.</p><p>In June, U.S. District Judge Manish Shah <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/06/30/jawad-fakroune-federal-prosecutors-fbi-pritzker" target="_blank" >sentenced Fakroune to 78 months in prison</a>, calling him a “lawless, violent bully.” Prosecutors described Fakroune’s pursuit of Garcia as a yearslong “campaign of terror.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Wacker Drive on Jan. 18, 2014.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>His criminal saga also produced one lingering mystery.</p><p>When FBI agents raided Fakroune’s New York apartment in December 2024, they found two Glock pistols that had been reported stolen. Fakroune’s lawyer later said the weapons <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/06/20/jawad-fakroune-chicago-police-department-extortion" target="_blank" >belonged to a Chicago police officer</a> who had falsely reported them stolen.</p><p>The Chicago Police Department’s Bureau of Internal Affairs opened an investigation but closed it <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/21/jawad-fakroune-chicago-police-department" target="_blank" >without determining the officer’s identity</a>.</p><p>Fakroune wasn’t around when the federal agents found the guns. He’d slipped away from the FBI during the raid and fled through Manhattan wearing little more than a black garbage bag, according to prosecutors. Agents caught him a month later at a rental home in Michigan City, Indiana.</p><p>Fakroune cultivated an image as a globe-trotting businessman and falsely boasted to people that he was a son of Pablo Escobar, the notorious Colombian cocaine kingpin.</p><p>Fakroune is a Moroccan national. He arrived in New York in 2001 in the federal diversity visa program, also known as the green-card lottery, which is open to people from countries with low immigration rates to the United States.</p><p>In 2008, he was convicted in New York of identity theft and bribery and served about four years in prison.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Kendall Gill, Will Perdue, Scott Williams, Robbie Hummel expected to be in Bulls' TV-analyst rotation
entries.summary: <p>Kendall Gill, Will Perdue, Scott Williams and Robbie Hummel are expected to be in the rotation to replace the late Stacey King as Bulls TV analyst alongside play-by-play voice Adam Amin, the Sun-Times has learned.</p><p>Gill is a longtime Bulls studio analyst who will take his first crack at being an NBA game analyst. Perdue, who worked with Gill in the studio and shared the NBA G League Windy City Bulls analyst job with him, was an analyst beside the late Jim Durham on ESPN Radio.</p><p>Williams has been a college and NBA analyst, and he's expected to continue in his college role at ESPN. Hummel likely would have the fewest games because of his national obligations with Big Ten Network, CBS, NBC and Turner, for whom he works college and NBA games. He has filled in on Bulls broadcasts before.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports/2026/07/16/how-chicago-bulls-might-tv-analyst-stacey-king-kendall-gill-robbie-hummel-sarah-kustok-will-perdue-scott-williams-michael-reinsdorf-nba-chicago-sports-network" >How Bulls might replace late TV analyst Stacey King — here are 5 candidates</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>King died at his home June 7 at age 59. He had been the Bulls' TV analyst for 20 years, entertaining fans with his humor, wit and trademark sayings. The Bulls have been expected to rotate analysts, at least in the first season after King's death, to alleviate the pressure of replacing him and audition analysts for a permanent job.</p><p>The Bulls return this fall for their third season on Chicago Sports Network, which is scheduled to air all but three of the team's 82 games. The season opener is Oct. 21 at Toronto, and the home opener is Oct. 24 against the Wizards, both on CHSN.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-8f0005" name="list-8f0005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageNumber=1, inverseColors=false, footerBgColor=#000000, bodyFont=font-3, showListNumbers=false, imagePositionHorizontal=null, pageCount=2925, rteBodyFont=font-3, previousPageLink=null, headerBottomBorderColor=#111010, subTitle=null, stickyHeader=true, listTitleColor=#000000, tableCellBorderColor=#ccd1d5, relatedListFont=font-1, hideAuthors=true, tertiaryTextColor=#6c6c6c, buttonHoverTextColor=#ffffff, tableFont=font-1, carouselAutoPlay=false, promoTitleFont=font-2, _styledTemplate=/page/list/PageListH.hbs, ctaButtonText=[], primaryTextColor=#2a2a2a, buttonTextColor=#ffffff, linkTextColor=#1a1a1a, hideTitles=false, footerLinkColor=#ffffff, carouselSpeed=null, items=[{type=Image, media=[{ampLink=null, _styledTemplate=null, _template=/image/Image.hbs, alt=Noa Essengue, image={src=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/b8/7c/f6fa7c264a178f59fffda968b24b/2242304038.jpg, width=4200, height=2800}, narrowImage={src=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/b8/7c/f6fa7c264a178f59fffda968b24b/2242304038.jpg, width=4200, height=2800}}], _styledTemplate=null, publishDate=August 30, 2026 07:41 AM, timestamp=1788093685000, imageAlignment=null, description=[{items=[Fall camp is less than a month away for the Bulls but players will start showing up to the Advocate Center for scrimmages and workouts over the course of that time. entries.title: Mayor Johnson projects $882M deficit, vows to not balance budget 'on backs of working people'
entries.summary: <p>Chicago faces a $882.4 million budget gap next year, Mayor Brandon Johnson announced Thursday as he teed up his next fight for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/22/advisory-referendums-city-council-battle-opposition-aldermen-mayor-brandon-johnson-tension" >“tax-the-rich” funding streams</a> he believes are needed to offset the city’s severe financial woes.</p><p>“We will not balance this budget on the backs of working people,” Johnson said as he released his annual budget forecast. “We will continue to fight for progressive, equitable revenues that ask those who can afford to contribute more to actually do more, while protecting the essential services Chicagoans depend on.”</p><p>The budget gap is not unexpected and is smaller than anticipated, officials said. But it is still one of the largest deficits in the city’s history, forcing yet another season of contentious conversations between Johnson and the Council over how to close it.</p><p>Last year, the city had to close a $1.2 billion gap to balance its roughly $17 billion budget.</p><p>Johnson, who did not directly rule out a property tax hike Thursday, will need to find efficiencies and revenue as he contends with an emboldened Council opposition that has rejected his boldest progressive pushes so far.</p><p>Johnson said the budget gap — again one of the city’s largest of the past two and a half decades — is driven in part by $70 million more in the city’s bond payments, $90 million more in pension obligations, cost-of-living adjustments for union workers, and commodity price hikes linked to the U.S. war against Iran, including $32 million more in fuel and energy costs.</p><p>Also driving the gap is the loss of one-time revenue sources crafted by City Council members in the 2026 budget and a reduced surplus of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/10/21/brandon-johnson-2026-budget-chicago-record-tif-surplus" >special tax dollars known as TIF funding</a>, Johnson said.</p><p>Currently, the city is expects to tap roughly $330 million to $340 million in surplus funds from special taxing districts. That’s far below <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" >the amount Chicago Public Schools is relying on to balance its budget.</a> The school district receives more than 50% of declared surpluses.</p><h3>Cost drivers </h3><p>The forecast is a preview of Johnson’s comprehensive budget proposal expected in the fall. It does not include specific ideas for how to close the gap, or the programs and city services Johnson plans to spend money on next year.</p><p>But Johnson revealed some of the costs driving the gap.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/brandon-johnson/2026/07/07/johnson-mid-year-budget-claims-131-7m-shortfall" >Chicago midyear budget claims $131.7M shortfall</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>For instance, the city is attempting to project the full cost of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/05/14/city-council-finance-committee-police-settlements-jon-burge-car-chases" >legal settlements, largely for police misconduct.</a> Routinely, the city has underestimated payouts, and then ends up spending double or triple the budgeted amount.</p><p>At an estimated $400 million for 2027, that new projection is the “largest driver of our increased financial costs,” next year, said acting budget director Jonathan Ernst.</p><p>“We want to be very transparent about the costs of these settlements and judgments that are related to actions that occurred decades ago,” he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-670000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Arnold Day, a wrongfully convicted man who spent 26 years in prison, received a $13.5 million settlement linked to the actions of officers working for former police Commander Jon Burge. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file photo</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The city will also earmark $364 million in a supplemental payment towards its retirement funds for workers, on top of the $2.97 billion payment requirement by state law.</p><p>Similar to making an extra payment on a credit card, the supplemental pension payment is a former Mayor Lori Lightfoot-era policy that is lauded by ratings agencies.</p><p>Johnson has stuck with the policy, though he attempted to reduce the supplemental payment to $121 million amid financial woes last year but was thwarted by opposition Council members who took control of the budget process.</p><p>Overall, Johnson said Thursday, he will have made $1.1 billion in supplemental pension payments by the end of this year.</p><h3>Political battle ahead </h3><p>This budget season is sure to mark yet another politically divisive battle between Johnson and his City Council opposition of mostly moderate and conservative alderpeople he has labeled the “corporate caucus.”</p><p>United against the mayor’s failed 2026 corporate head tax proposal, the Council passed <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/12/23/mayor-brandon-johnson-city-council-alternate-budget" >a series of alternative revenue fixes</a> that have yet to produce much cash, including a proposal staunchly opposed by Johnson to sell old city debt to private collectors.</p><p>Johnson’s financial team said the 2027 budget completely nixes that projected $89 million revenue stream, after failed debt-buying deals with two different banks. The budget will assume some revenue from another Council idea — selling ad space on city bridges, said Ernst.</p><p>“It's not as though we never said the advertising couldn't bring in anything,” Ernst said. “It's the timing … we knew it would take time, and the number seemed off. It seemed far, far too high. So we're assuming some revenue, but significantly lower than what was projected for ‘26.” </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1b0000" name="image-1b0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9be4121/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7582x4255+0+401/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe0%2F9c%2F93f4cbde4445ba087d27291893f7%2Fmayorbudget-101725-37.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f6a1cb8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7582x4255+0+401/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe0%2F9c%2F93f4cbde4445ba087d27291893f7%2Fmayorbudget-101725-37.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/39fad4c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7582x4255+0+401/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe0%2F9c%2F93f4cbde4445ba087d27291893f7%2Fmayorbudget-101725-37.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Some alderpeople give a standing ovation after Mayor Brandon Johnson presented his budget for the 2026 fiscal year at a Chicago City Council meeting at City Hall on Thursday, Oct. 16, 2025. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/39fad4c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7582x4255+0+401/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe0%2F9c%2F93f4cbde4445ba087d27291893f7%2Fmayorbudget-101725-37.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fe412a2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7582x4255+0+401/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe0%2F9c%2F93f4cbde4445ba087d27291893f7%2Fmayorbudget-101725-37.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/39fad4c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7582x4255+0+401/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe0%2F9c%2F93f4cbde4445ba087d27291893f7%2Fmayorbudget-101725-37.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Some alderpeople gave Mayor Brandon Johnson a standing ovation after he presented his 2026 budget, but that budget immediately hit a wall of opposition from some Council members who eventually pushed through an alternative budget, which eventually took effect.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Council coalition, which also fought for a larger supplemental pension payment, has remained organized and is unlikely to back down anytime soon. But<b> </b>Finance Committee chair Pat Dowell (3rd) said she’s trying to remain optimistic.</p><p>She said the coalition does not plan to introduce their own proposal to counter Johnson’s right off the bat, in favor of collaboration.</p><p>“But that’s really up to the mayor if he wants to collaborate or not,” Dowell said. “I would hope that he realizes from last year that the City Council is a co-equal branch of government.” </p><p>Johnson heads into this budget season with a brand new fiscal team after a series of high-profile departures.</p><p>But his new <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/11/mayor-brandon-johnson-new-chief-financial-officer-ashlee-gabrysch" target="_blank" ><u>CFO, Ashlee Gabrysch</u></a>, is a former senior director at Fitch Ratings where she served as the agency’s lead analyst for both Chicago and Illinois. She could help bridge the divide between the mayor and an emboldened opposition that had grown distrusting, and at times outright irreverent, toward Johnson’s now-gone budget leaders.</p><h3>Closing the 2027 gap</h3><p>Johnson, expected to announce his reelection campaign Sept. 13, is likely to embark on yet another mission to pass progressive revenue in his fourth, and potentially final, budget.</p><p>By simply pitching a new tax on wealthy Chicagoans, Johnson would be daring City Council members, many of whom are seeking another term themselves, to reject a “tax-the-rich” measure at a time when voters are demanding affordability.</p><p>It’s unclear whether Johnson will pitch a new revenue stream, another corporate head tax, or double down on the types of revenue he has already passed. Those include a tax on cloud computing that's overperforming by $41 million this year. </p><p>Taxes on social media companies and online sports betting are also raking in cash and outperforming initial estimates by 56% and 69%, respectively. But both are facing a court challenge.</p><p>“'I’ve kept my commitment to challenging corporations and those with means to put more skin in the game. Obviously, with the forecast, it's demonstrating that it's working,” Johnson said. “When I present my budget in a little bit over a month, you can anticipate that that will remain my focus.”</p><p>Johnson did not explicitly rule out increasing property tax. But he and the City Council have likely missed their window to do so. The politically unpopular revenue driver is likely to be dead-on-arrival in an election year. The Council has already shown its distaste for the idea by unanimously rejecting Johnson’s proposed $300 million property tax hike in his 2025 budget.</p><p>The forecast also predicts worsening budget gaps in the years to come, growing to $943 million in 2028, and $1.02 billion in 2029.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure
