class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times file </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>TIF surplus </h3><p>Johnson issued record TIF surpluses in his first three budgets, but that well is starting to run dry, and 2027 could be the lowest declared surplus of his tenure. </p><p>TIF funding is made up of incremental increases in property tax revenue that get set aside for local development projects, rather than going towards schools, libraries, parks or the city’s checking account. State law requires excess funds at the end of each year to be distributed among those local taxing bodies. The city gets roughly 23% of that surplus, while Chicago Public Schools receives around 55%.</p><p>This year, CPS is relying on at least $285 million in TIF funds to balance its own shaky financial picture, though that could grow by $150 million if the state doesn’t come through with more money. That would require the city to declare anywhere between a $518 million to $790 million surplus. Currently, the city is projecting up to $340 million.</p><p>Johnson has been able to issue such large TIF surpluses in part because most TIF districts were created in the 1980s and 1990s and have been reaching a peak of taxable revenue. It’s also because of a Johnson administration rule prohibiting alderpeople from indefinitely earmarking TIF funds for future projects, instead limiting them to one year.</p><p>Critics have slammed Johnson for relying on one-time TIF surpluses to balance the city’s budget. The Civic Federation, a budget watchdog, has said the city “has benefited from increasingly large TIF sweeps in recent years” but warns TIF surpluses have become a “stealth property tax” that will soon start to decline.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/26/tif-tax-increment-financing-property-taxes-chicago-uic-great-cities-institute" >Chicago program that set aside billions for development has left poor areas behind, UIC study finds</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Top 5 moments from Bears QB Caleb Williams' 'Hot Ones' debut
entries.summary: <p>Before he began the hot wing gauntlet on the popular streaming show “Hot Ones,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/halas-intrigue/2026/09/01/bears-kyler-gordon-podcast-halas-intrigue" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> took a few deep breaths.</p><p>“That’s typically what I do before a two-minute drill,” he said.</p><p>Williams, who was known for his last-minute comebacks last year, went on to master all 10 wings put in front him — all while conducting an interview with host Sean Evans.</p><p>Williams, who lost weight during the offseason, joked Tuesday that he did the show months ago on a “cheat day.”</p><p>“It was hot as [expletive],” he said. “No, it was a good time. He asked good questions, but yeah, you can count it as a cheat day. It was a good day.”</p><p>Here are the top five things we learned from his interview:</p><h3>1. He didn’t know if he’d like Chicago at first.</h3><p>Williams and Evans — who attended Crystal Lake Central High School and the U. of I., and is a lifelong Bears fans — bonded over the quarterback’s love of the city. Truth be told, though, Williams wasn’t sure he’d love Chicago as much as he has.</p><p>“I didn’t think I was gonna like it that much, to be honest,” he said. “And I fell in love with the city of Chicago, the people, the food. Obviously the sports. … I’ve got a couple other friends playing in Chicago sports — [the Cubs’] PCA, [the Bulls’] Matas [Buzelis], other guys. …</p><p>“The people I would say is the biggest thing. I didn’t realize the people were so hospitable. Also Chicago is insanely clean. That surprised me.</p><h3>2. Ben Johnson is part mentor, part partner</h3><h3></h3><p>When Williams was asked to describe his relationship with Johnson, he said he was part mentor — given how hard he coaches him during the week — and part jazz partner.</p><p>“The jazz part is typically on Sunday,” he said. “You get on the field and it becomes poetic, it becomes a good ole jazz night.”</p><h3>3. Receiver Jahdae Walker never shuts up.</h3><p>“You hear Jahdae Walker when you wake up,” Williams said. “You hear him when you go to sleep.”</p><p>He identified other teammate superlatives, saying tight end Cole Kmet and defensive tackle Grady Jarrett would be good head coaches; quarterback Case Keenum had the smartest football mind; and that Walker and Luther Burden had the best touchdown celebrations.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/n69BsyEKV_0?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Caleb Williams Has Ice in His Veins While Eating Spicy Wings | Hot Ones"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3>4. Milk was a good choice</h3><p>Williams plowed through the wings as they got increasingly spicier — from 2,100 Scoville units to 7,900 to 18,000 to 32,000 to 54,000 to 69,000 to 102,000. He began to struggle with the third-to-last wing, which was scored a 135,600 on the scale, which measures capsaicinoids.</p><p>“That’s the hot one, isn’t it?” he asked, choking up.</p><p>When the next wing was presented — at 820,000 Scoville units — he winced.</p><p>“We got more milk?” he asked.</p><p>The final wing had a Scoville scale of “TBA,” which is scary enough. Williams took a swig of milk — “Shout out, dairy!” he said — and took a bite. He stood and raised his hands like a victorious boxer.</p><h3>5. He wants to be the best</h3><h3></h3><p>Williams was asked to break down what made the following quarterbacks great:</p><p>• Randall Cunningham: “Cannon. He could do the thing I did versus the Rams from 20 extra yards.”</p><p>• Tom Brady: “Two-minute Killer. End-of-game. Moment-Killer.”</p><p>• Aaron Rodgers: “Magician with the football.”</p><p>And how about Williams himself?</p><p>“All of the above,” Williams, who's never been short of confidence, said with a laugh.<br></p>

entries.title: Trump administration pushes to remove tax exemption for private colleges with DEI policies
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is proposing a new rule that would strip private schools and colleges of their <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/harvard-nonprofit-tax-exempt-status-how-can-it-be-revoked-096614ea5ec65ec7a6ac08efd0f1e94f" target="_blank" >tax-exempt status</a> if they provide targeted help to students based on their race, a significant escalation in the White House's campaign to <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/dei-critical-race-theory-colleges-diversity-db8317ad37931558dd5a396cf5ab3d42" target="_blank" >eradicate diversity programs</a> directed at Black, Hispanic and other minority students.</p><p>The Treasury Department proposed the change Thursday in a new regulation that, if made final, would kick in after May 2027. The rule is broadly aimed at ending any policies or programs that help students because of their race, and it specifically says such benefits in admissions, scholarships and facilities “would be incompatible” with the rule.</p><p>It’s the latest attempt by the Trump administration to pressure schools and colleges to weed out diversity, equity and inclusion policies that had become common before President Donald Trump returned to the White House with a <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-woke-education-24f864d83e2f5745d12a79ebac0d7cc4" target="_blank" >promise to end them</a>. Trump officials have used Civil Rights-era laws to unwind the policies, saying they discriminate against white and Asian American students.</p><p>Scores of universities have <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/dei-diversity-equity-inclusion-college-bbe09c081d8a47fcb5616c8fa3b23cee" target="_blank" >shut down or rebranded</a> their DEI offices and ended scholarships and clubs designed for minority students under pressure from the White House. In a statement announcing the proposal, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested that even policies that are no longer under the banner of DEI could be targeted.</p><p>“Schools rebranding race-based preferences as equitable, inclusive, or diversity-enhancing does not change their discriminatory nature,” Bessent said.</p><p>The Treasury Department and IRS estimate that up to 18,000 private schools, colleges and other education institutions could be affected by the proposal.</p><p>America’s private universities have been exempt from many taxes for more than a century because they provide a public good. The benefit saves many universities millions of dollars every year.</p><p>Trump has seen the tax-exempt status as a lever to pull in his pressure campaign against colleges that he describes as hotbeds of “wokeness.” He threatened to cut the benefit for Harvard University last year during his battle with the nation’s oldest college. In a response, Harvard officials said there was no legal basis for doing so and argued it would force cuts to financial aid and crucial medical research.</p><p>It’s incredibly rare for the federal government to go after a college’s tax-exempt status, but there’s one notable precedent. Bob Jones University, a small Christian school in South Carolina, lost the benefit in the 1970s over a ban on interracial dating and marriage on campus. The Supreme Court upheld the IRS’s decision to deny the school its exemption. The school has since ended the ban and regained tax-exempt status in 2017.</p><p>Laws forbid the IRS from targeting individuals and organizations for ideological reasons, and federal officials are not allowed to direct IRS investigations.</p><p>To maintain nonprofit status, which allows donations to be tax-deductible, organizations must follow IRS rules on lobbying, political campaign activity and annual reporting requirements, as well as other obligations.</p><p>The Trump administration describes the new proposal as a move toward restoring merit in the nation’s education systems.</p><p>The Justice Department has separately opened investigations into several <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-medical-school-stanford-ohio-state-a7d892267d74cc798167fb48379f7f6d" target="_blank" >medical schools</a> that it accuses of favoring Black and Hispanic students in admissions. Trump officials say any such favoritism violates Title IV of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, a federal law that forbids discrimination in education and was created to fight segregation and its impact.</p><p>A statement from IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano said private schools that promote discriminatory practices will no longer be exempt from taxes.</p><p>“Today’s proposed regulations put institutions on notice and schools that continue to engage in racial discrimination should expect to lose that status,” he said.</p><p>___</p><p>Associated Press Education Writer Annie Ma contributed to this report.</p><p>___</p><p>The Associated Press’ education coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. AP is solely responsible for all content. entries.title: Star receiver James Skokna is the youngest in a string of seven brothers to play for Hinsdale Central
entries.summary: <p>James Skokna waited a while for his turn at suiting up for Hinsdale Central.</p><p>The youngest of 10 siblings, all six of Skokna’s older brothers played football.</p><p>“I’ve been watching Hinsdale Central football all my life. It’s why I love football so much,” Skokna said. “Growing up I always dreamed of playing for the Red Devils. Now that I’ve got to, it’s nothing short of what I dreamed of.”</p><p>Now in his third varsity season, the senior is on track to break every Hinsdale Central receiving record.</p><p>“That would be pretty cool but I can’t say I’m too worried about it,” Skokna said. “I’m more worried if the team wins or not. But that would be cool.”</p><p>Skokna through two weeks this season has 16 catches for 195 yards and two touchdowns heading into Hinsdale Central’s West Suburban Silver opener against fellow unbeaten Downers Grove North on Friday in Hinsdale.</p><p>He had 25 catches for 431 yards and five TDs as a sophomore with 509 yards. Last season, Skokna had 53 catches for 770 yards and six TDs, with 487 return yards.</p><p>“He’s so consistent with how he takes care of himself, how he approaches the game. He’s done everything in his power to make his body as strong and physically fit as he can. He’s a workhorse,” Hinsdale Central coach Brian Griffin said. “He’s not flashy about it. He just goes out there, does the work, gets the hard yards and the big plays.”</p><p>Growing up, Skokna played running back and cornerback. He switched to receiver in eighth grade and didn’t look back. Skokna lines up split wide or in the slot, returns punts and kicks and will even jump in at cornerback when needed.</p><p>“He’s so explosive when he catches the ball,” Griffin said. “It’s the plays he makes beyond running the routes that aren’t coachable that he makes pretty routinely. You get used to it. That is what separates him.”</p><h3>IC Catholic QB Nate Lang off to flying start</h3><p>Nate Lang has picked up right where he left off.</p><p>IC Catholic Prep’s quarterback threw for over 2,400 yards and 28 touchdowns as a junior, helping lead the Knights to the Class 3A quarterfinals.</p><p>Through two games this fall, Lang has thrown for 527 yards and seven TDs with zero interceptions. IC Catholic, with a large group of returning starters led by Power Four prospect Grant Bowen, is one of nine remaining Catholic League unbeatens.</p><p>“I feel like we are really starting to catch a rhythm,” Lang said. “We have a lot of returning starters from last year on both sides of the ball. We’re starting to get back into rhythm.”</p><p>Lang completed 69.4% of his passes with just four interceptions as a junior, and is at a 70.8% completion rate so far this year.</p><p>“I have a lot of good chemistry with my receivers. They have trust in me and I have trust in them,” Lang said. “That makes my life easier, and knowing I have trust in my coaches that they will dial up the right plays.”</p><p>As good as the Knights’ offense was last year, it could be even better now.</p><p>Lang was IC Catholic’s leading rusher as a junior, but sophomore Jakobe Baldwin went over 200 yards rushing in the Knights’ season-opening win over Nazareth and is at 9.3 yards per carry through two games.</p><p>“It definitely helps a lot,” Lang said. “Jakobe burst onto the scene that first game, surprised a lot of people. I have a lot of confidence in his ability, him and our O-line.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.shawlocal.com/friday-night-drive/" target="_blank" >Read more high school football coverage at Friday Night Drive.</a></p>

entries.title: Celebrate jobs — while we still have them — on Labor Day
entries.summary: <p>We lose jobs, find jobs, love jobs, hate them, sometimes all at once.</p><p>A lucky few snag their dream, early, then work with growing satisfaction and success.</p><p>But most of us are like English poet Philip Larkin who, at 31, was stuck in his fourth year as an assistant librarian. He saw his job as a fat frog, plopped atop his true spirit, crushing it, and wrote the poem "Toads," which begins:</p><p> Why should I let the toad work<br> Squat on my life?<br> Can’t I use my wit as a pitchfork<br> And drive the brute off?</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9f0000" name="module-9f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>No, he couldn't. Larkin was a librarian for 30 years. We need that job, Larkin writes, "Just for paying a few bills."</p><p>With Labor Day this Monday, and the future of employment in question, thanks to AI and other disruptions, it might be worth pausing to consider the central role work holds in our lives.</p><p>Our jobs define us. You can't call someone "a housewife" in an obituary anymore — it's considered demeaning. She "manages a household." But nobody is "a person who plumbs." We are plumbers, accountants, newspaper columnists.</p><p>We also define our jobs, if we can, molding them to our purposes.</p><p>"At first I was impressed with the time he spent in his office, arriving early and leaving late," said Larkin's employer. "It was only later that I realized that his office was also his study where he spent hours on his private writing as well as the work of the library."</p><p>For many, a job is the most significant part of their lives, second — maybe — to family. In that light, Labor Day should be more than a long weekend. It should be a big celebration, and once was, with Labor Day parades filled with professions, proud street sweepers in their dress whites, carrying their brooms like rifles.</p><p>But machines sweep streets. Technology, that great job killer, looms over employment, threatening "the AI jobs apocalypse." Half of white-collar jobs could be taken over by AI, according to Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, with unemployment at 20%. Some think that view too dire.</p><p>An old story in a new realm. Automation scythes through work. At the last brick company in the Chicago area, the Glen-Gary brickworks, “nobody touches the brick; it’s all computerized." A few decades ago Glen-Gary had about 240 employees. Now they only need 24.</p><p>My job puts me in contact with all sorts of occupations, and I'm frequently awed at how satisfied people are doing work that would put me cowering in a corner. Once I watched a man stand in a refrigerated room, running his bare hand over whitefish filets, pulling out pin bones with a needle nose pliers. He'd been at it seven years, and was grateful to be in this country, working. The immigrants at Cologuard, up in Madison, whose jobs are to open jars of excrement and test the contents for cancer, consider themselves on the forefront of medicine and are proud of saving lives. Harry Heftman ran the hot dog stand at Randolph and Orleans for more than 50 years, and was the most upbeat man I ever met. </p><p>Me, I worked behind the counter for a few minutes at the cafeteria at Vienna Beef as part their two day Hot Dog U, could barely keep the orders straight, and wanted to kiss the ground when I got back to my office.</p><p>I suppose I would have gotten good at it, over time. That's one of the joys of working — we develop skills. I have an unusual job, on several metrics. I've been at it a long time — 40 years this coming March. The median stint at a company for an American employee is four years.</p><p>How'd I last that long? The union helped. I'm a quick study. Freedom is always cited as important in a job, and I have latitude over what goes into this space. I could have asked AI to snap out this column in an eyeblink, and maybe next year someone will. Maybe I'll be one of the bench sitters Larkin considers in "Toads Revisited,"</p><p> Being one of the men<br> You meet of an afternoon:<br> Palsied old step-takers,</p><p>Guys who are:</p><p> Watching the bread delivered...<br> Think of being them,<br> Turning over their failures</p><p>Larkin, older, sees work in a new light. The poem ends.</p><p> Give me your arm, old toad;<br> Help me down Cemetery Road.</p><p>That's a bleak finish. I often quote Noel Coward's breezy, "Work is more fun than fun." Then again, work for Coward was gazing at the blue Caribbean, nursing a cocktail and coining witty lines for his next play. </p><p>We all do what we can, and what we must. A lucky few even do what we want.</p>
entries.author: Neil Steinberg

entries.title: Will Notre Dame make easy work of Wisconsin at Lambeau Field?
entries.summary: <p>It has been nine months since the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >College Football</a> Playoff selection committee took the old conceit that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >Notre Dame</a> always gets special treatment, wadded it into a ball and punted it into the ether.</p><p>What, you forgot already?</p><p>Quick review: The Irish were ranked No. 10 at 10-2, right behind Alabama and ahead of Miami. Alabama then got smoked in the SEC championship game for its third loss, while the Irish and Miami were idle. That’s when the committee rolled up its sleeves, cracked its knuckles, took a long swig of coffee, snuffed out its cigarette and (1) left Alabama right where it was, (2) bumped Miami up to 10 and (3) told the Irish to take a hike.</p><p>No playoff for a team most would agree was plenty good enough to do some damage, whether it truly deserved a shot at it or not.</p><p>Yes, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2025/12/07/notre-dame-left-out-of-college-football-playoff-declines-bowl-consideration" target="_blank" >those Irish had an all-time beef</a>.</p><p>But this year’s team has the schedule to more than make up for it, starting with the opener at Lambeau Field, home of the Green Bay Packers.</p><p>If <b>No. 4 Notre Dame (-20½) vs. Wisconsin </b>(6:30 p.m. Sunday, NBC 5, 780-AM) doesn’t have the feel of a particularly daunting opening-game assignment for the Irish, it’s probably because it isn’t. Down the line come a game at North Carolina, a trip to BYU, a rematch with Miami — this time in South Bend — and a visit by SMU. That’s the hard stuff, as it looks now. If the Irish are as strong as their reputation heading into the season, they’ll be favored in every game and in most of them by double digits.</p><p>In other words, anyone rooting for the Irish’s first national title since 1988 should be embracing the mantra, “This could be the year. No, really. Yeah, I know I’ve said that at least 15 other years, but this time I mean it.”</p><p>The offense should light up scoreboards, with quarterback CJ Carr positioned to contend for the Heisman Trophy. The defense should be one of the stingiest out there, with cornerback Leonard Moore locking things down and Boubacar Traore terrorizing opposing passers.</p><p>Fun facts: Wisconsin coach Luke Fickell was Irish coach Marcus Freeman’s position coach at Ohio State, where Freeman was a standout linebacker, and Freeman later became a rising star as Fickell’s defensive coordinator at Cincinnati.</p><p>“I wouldn’t be in this position without the investment he made in me,” Freeman said this week.</p><p>Not-so-fun fact, if you’re Fickell: “Hot seat” is an understatement after seven-, five- and four-win seasons for the Badgers.</p><p>The Badgers have a dual-threat transfer QB, Colton Joseph, who rushed for over 1,000 yards at Old Dominion last season. Here’s hoping Joseph avoids the injury fate shared by each of Fickell’s last three transfer QB1s at the school, Tanner Mordecai, Tyler Van Dyke and Billy Edwards Jr.</p><p>Something to keep in mind: Freeman has been on the wrong end of more than one giant early-season upset at Notre Dame. Losing this game would add to the list.</p><p>Not happening, though. Irish, 27-14.</p><p><b>OTHER WEEK 1 PICKS</b></p><p><i>All games are Saturday unless otherwise noted.</i></p><p><b>Toledo (+10½) at Michigan State </b>(7 p.m. Friday, FS1): It’s Game 1 of the rest of Pat Fitzgerald’s life, or at least the rest of his time coaching the Spartans. Fitzgerald’s Northwestern teams often were slow starters, and the early going at MSU figures to be bumpy. Opening with Toledo might be good timing, though, considering the Rockets are in major transition mode themselves. Go Green, 24-21.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">It takes everybody. <a href="https://t.co/EnV75EoV9b">pic.twitter.com/EnV75EoV9b</a></p>— Michigan State Football (@MSU_Football) <a href="https://x.com/MSU_Football/status/2093813443854033137?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 29, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p><b>Northern Illinois (+31½) at No. 22 Iowa </b>(3:15 p.m., BTN): The Hawkeyes have all sorts of questions to answer on offense — insert wisecrack here — but NIU, with an interim coach in Rob Harley now that Thomas Hammock is busy coaching running backs in the NFL, might not offer much in the way of resistance. Huskies go down hard, 34-6.</p><p><b>South Dakota State (+13½) at Northwestern </b>(7 p.m., BTN, 720-AM): Let’s see what new offensive coordinator Chip Kelly cooks up with transfer QB Aidan Chiles. Can the Wildcats amp things up on the ol’ excitement-o-meter as they near the opening of their new stadium? Watch out for the Jackrabbits, one of the powerhouse programs of the FCS. Cats sweat out a 31-21 “W.”</p><p><b>No. 9 Ole Miss (-6½) vs. No. 24 Louisville </b>(6:30 p.m. Sunday, ABC 7): Nashville, Tenn., will see a heck of a show from both lightning-fast offenses, but how do you not roll with Rebels QB Trinidad Chambliss, one of the brightest stars of last season’s playoff? Score one for the SEC, 34-27.</p><p>My favorite favorite: <b>No. 11 LSU (-10½) vs. Clemson </b>(6:30 p.m., ABC 7): Which Tigers? Which Death Valley? No need to ask — 100,000 screaming maniacs in purple and gold will give it away. Bayou Bengals open the Lane Kiffin era with a bang.</p><p>My favorite underdog: <b>California (+1½) vs. UCLA </b>(9:30 p.m., ESPN): Just because Bob Chesney followed Curt Cignetti at James Madison, it definitely doesn’t mean he’s getting ready to pull a Cignetti with the Bruins. Score one for the — wait, which conference is Cal in again? — ACC.</p><p><b>Last season’s record: </b>76-30 straight-up, 53-52-1 against the spread.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/09/02/big-ten-football-preview-ohio-state-oregon-indiana-michigan-illinois-northwestern-cfb" target="_blank" >Big Ten football preview: Ohio State, Oregon or Indiana at the top? Where do Illinois, Northwestern come in?</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2025/12/07/notre-dame-left-out-of-college-football-playoff-declines-bowl-consideration" target="_blank" >Notre Dame, left out of College Football Playoff, declines bowl consideration</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: USA Dodgeball National Championships to draw top players to Bedford Park this weekend
entries.summary: <p>The nation's best dodge ball players are set to descend upon Chicago.</p><p>The USA Dodgeball National Championships will take place Friday, Saturday and Sunday at the Wintrust Sports Complex in Bedford Park, just south of Midway Airport.</p><p>The event is free for spectators to come check out, and there's a bar at the facility (not free).</p><p>More than 500 players will compete in categories across gender and ball type.</p><p>There are three different types of balls, each about seven inches in diameter, making them slightly smaller than the red rubber balls popularly used in grade school gym class.</p><p>Friday will feature no-sting balls (a mini version of that familiar red rubber ball).</p><p>Saturday will feature foam balls (made out of a light weight memory foam).</p><p>Sunday will feature cloth balls (similar in feel to a volleyball).</p><p>Top teams use foam balls that travel at speeds exceeding 80 m.p.h.</p><p>"Dodgeball at this level is like a chess game," said Dustin Harwood, who's on the leadership team of USA Dodgeball, a nonprofit. "It's very strategic. It's not like in gym class growing up where there's one guy who played baseball or one girl who played softball who can eliminate everybody." </p><p>The tournament runs each day from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. and will feature simultaneous games on multiple courts, some of which will be live streamed on the YouTube channel <a class="Link" href="https://dodgeball.live/" target="_blank" >dodgeball.live</a> with volunteer commentators.</p><p>The sports top talent uses foam balls.</p><p>The reigning national champs in foam are the Outsiders, a team that draws players mainly from Dallas, but includes a members from other parts of the country, including Chicago resident Bo Tillmon, 36.</p><p>"One of our main strategies is to utilize our athleticism, wait for our opponents to throw, then sprint after them as they're retreating and hit them," said Tillmon, who works at Salesforce and lives in Ukrainian Village.</p><p>People generally react with incredulity when Tillmon tells them about his hobby (and it is just a hobby; top players have day jobs and do not earn a living playing dodgeball).</p><p>"People are like 'What?'" said Tillmon. "I usually don't like to talk about it a lot in public because then you have to explain the whole thing, and show a video, but then people are like 'Oh' and they see it's a legitimate sport and not what we played as kids."</p><p>USA Dodgeball formed in 2017 and has about 12,000 players in member organizations around the country, with about 1,000 playing at an elite level and traveling to compete in tournaments around the country.</p><p>The vast majority play recreationally to meet people and socialize after games.</p><p>Matt De La Cruz, 33, heads up Chicago Dodgeball, which plays at the Lake View YMCA and is a member organization of USA Dodgeball.</p><p>"The dodgeball community prides itself on being an inclusive community, and I love introducing people to it," said De La Cruz, a medical-device engineer who lives in Roscoe Village and is competing this weekend.</p><p>"There's a variety of experience. I used to play rugby, but people can join us with any sort of experience. It's just fun," he said. "I'd encourage people to come check us out. We have a Facebook page."</p><p><i>Find the complete schedule at </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.dodgeballhub.com/" target="_blank" ><i>dodgeballhub.com</i></a><i>.</i></p>
entries.author: Mitch Dudek

entries.title: SEC sues LSU, claiming the school recruited pro athletes against league rules
entries.summary: <p>BATON ROUGE, La. — The Southeastern Conference filed a lawsuit against LSU and its leadership in Alabama federal court on Thursday, alleging the school had "waged a deliberate and coordinated campaign to recruit professional athletes" against league rules.</p><p>The extraordinary step against one of the league's founding members came as SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey testified 400 miles away in a courtroom not far from Tiger Stadium, defending the league's ability to enforce its rules as several dozen athletes try to play this fall after they turned pro.</p><p>Former New Orleans Saints defensive lineman Zxavian Harris and former Cleveland Browns tight end Dae'Quan Wright sat next to each other in the gallery as the hearing began, with Sankey taking the stand a short time later..</p><p>The lawsuit asks for a court injunction barring LSU from violating the SEC's First Amendment rights by forcing it to "associate with conduct that is contrary to the conference's purpose and mission." It was filed in northern Alabama because the SEC is based in Birmingham.</p><p>Attorneys for the athletes, the NCAA and the SEC were appearing before East Baton Rouge Parish Judge William Jorden, who scheduled the hearing concerning the status of his earlier temporary injunction preventing the NCAA from ruling recent former pros or fifth-year college athletes ineligible — a stance also taken by the SEC and other Power Four conferences with formal rules adopted last week.</p><p>Jorden also wanted the NCAA to explain why it should not be held in contempt after the power conferences set up potential punishments of its member schools who place former NFL or NBA athletes on their football or basketball rosters.</p><p>The players in question also include former Denver Broncos defensive back Blake Cotton, who like Harris and Wright is hoping to join LSU and new coach Lane Kiffin.</p><p>Wright, who played for Kiffin last season at Mississippi, started practicing with at LSU this week, too late to be eligible for Saturday's home opener against Clemson under the NCAA's required seven days of practice. Harris, who also played at Ole Miss last season, has committed to LSU, while Cotton, who played at Utah last fall, has been recruited by Kiffin.</p><p>All three are among a host of athletes who've argued in lawsuits around the country that they are unfairly being denied an opportunity to spend a fifth year in college under newly adopted NCAA rules allowing for five full years of competition. In all, the NCAA says there are approximately 450 athlete plaintiffs seeking additional eligibility through litigation, with some 300 of them winning the ability to play at least for now and about 150 who have been rejected.</p><p>The athletes in the case who signed pro contracts have argued they did so only because current rules that would have allowed them another college season weren't adopted until after their decisions to leave for the chance to make an NFL roster.</p><p>The SEC filed a brief in the case on Wednesday in which it stated that the question before the judge should be a narrow one regarding whether the conference "can enforce and require its member institutions to comply with SEC rules." The SEC's proposed punishments include significant fines, up to half-season suspensions for coaches and member universities' loss of voting on privileges on league business matters.</p><p>Sankey provided an affidavit stating that SEC university presidents voted 15-0 in favor of the new rules, with LSU's Wade Rousse abstaining. Sankey also said the SEC was acting on its own and not attempting to collude with NCAA to stop Kiffin from bringing in ex-pros.</p><p>The fight over eligibility between schools, conferences and the NCAA has simmered for months and spilled into politics.</p><p>Georgia Attorney General Chris Carr reportedly sent a letter of support to Sankey, encouraging him to take "all measures available" to punish LSU if it added former NFL players to its 2026 roster of 105 players, which was due to be submitted to the SEC by Friday. He also criticized the judge's injunction.</p><p>"It is no coincidence that the very institution set to potentially use this temporary order to flout the SEC's rule is in the trial court's own backyard," Carr wrote.</p><p>Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill also weighed in, writing in a brief that the NCAA had subjected athletes in the case to a "classic bait-and-switch."</p><p>"The NCAA's ever-changing rules have consequences beyond these individual athletes," said Murrill, who attended the hearing and chatted with plaintiff attorneys before the proceeding. "They affect the universities that recruit them, the other student-athletes with whom they compete, and the coaches and administrators responsible for complying with an increasingly complicated set of rules."</p>

No other details were released.</p>

entries.title: The Sky need to help Gabriela Jaquez rediscover her hot start
entries.summary: <p>Gabriela Jaquez’s first four <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wnba" >WNBA</a> games made her look wise beyond her years.</p><p>The rookie made bold drives to the basket. She came up with steals in crucial moments. She did the little things, getting deflections and sprinting the floor in transition.</p><p>“This is no rookie,” veteran Natasha Cloud said after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> beat the Lynx on the road, complimenting Jaquez’s immediate grasp of the pro game.</p><p>The Sky were forming an identity that reflected players like Cloud and Jaquez — gritty underdogs, jacks-of-all-trades if masters of none. They were 3-1 then, and one could almost taste the victorious trajectory: Jaquez would prove she was a sleeper pick at No. 5, and the Sky would prove their roster retool had made them worthy of the playoffs.</p><p>The Sky’s unraveling will need to be studied for years to come. Jaquez’s fall-off is layered too, but a hyperextended knee in late May definitely knocked her off course.</p><p>By the time she returned from the injury, the Sky were in the depths of an eight-game losing streak.</p><p>She still drove hard into the paint, but seemed unsure whether to finish with a floater or pull up jumper. She generated fewer steals and was no longer always in the right place at the right time.</p><p>She looked more like a rookie. She was also treated more like one, or at least like a player who had not fully earned her coach’s trust.</p><p>At times, Jaquez was a steady part of the rotation. In other games, she played fewer than five minutes.</p><p>Unsurprisingly, her production declined. In her first 14 games, Jaquez averaged 9.7 points and 4.4 rebounds while shooting 33% from three-point range. Since June 26, she’s averaged only 4.4 points and two rebounds while shooting 19.4% from three.</p><p>Jaquez was asked this past Saturday about the challenge of establishing herself despite inconsistent playing time. She answered as she typically does: by demonstrating a growth mindset and a willingness to make the most of any opportunity.</p><p>“It’s not gonna be easy,” she said. “Nothing’s handed to you. Obviously, I have had my ups and downs, more playing time, less playing time. Knowing that every game’s gonna bring something different and I just have to stay ready. We have a lot of guards on this team, but when I go in, how can I make a difference? How can I bring a spark? That’s just my mentality.”</p><p>It’s a realistic, pro’s answer.</p><p>Still, the sudden reversal of fortune over the past five months has to be frustrating for the 22-year-old. In April, she won the national championship at UCLA, was drafted No. 5 and became a key contributor on a surprisingly good team.</p><p>Now there are four games left in the regular season, her team missed the playoffs and her role never solidified.</p><p>When pressed about Jaquez’s playing time, as coaches of lottery picks inevitably are, Tyler Marsh has said the inconsistency is not about her, per se. The Sky have a lot of guards, it is difficult to find minutes for everyone, and he has gone with whoever is playing well on a given night.</p><p>In Marsh’s defense, all of that is true. He has to respond to the flow of a game. But the moment the Sky were eliminated from the playoffs — almost a month ago now — he should have pivoted and prioritized Jaquez. Instead, her minutes have only increased meaningfully in the last two games.</p><p>It raises some harsh questions for the organization.</p><p>Should they have drafted another guard, such as Flau’jae Johnson or Kiki Rice, both of whom have produced more complete rookie seasons?</p><p>Or did the coaching staff mishandle her development or rattle her confidence?</p><p>Self-doubt about her recent struggles could be holding her back.</p><p>What Jaquez needs to remember is this: The player who came out of the gates with confidence — driving hard, disrupting passing lanes and doing all the little things — did not disappear.</p><p>The last four games of the regular season should be all about finding her again.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Tristan Peters' magical debut season continues with AL Rookie of the Month honors
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON — He’s already hit for a cycle, made the All-Star team, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/26/tristan-peters-white-sox-munetaka-murakami-colson-montgomery-franchise-record-frank-thomas-paul-konerko-carlos-lee-will-venable" target="_blank" ><u>homered in five consecutive games</u></a>, so winning American League rookie of the month for August shouldn’t feel like it’s breaking new ground for White Sox centerfielder <b>Tristan Peters</b>.</p><p>“The story of Tristan this year has been incredible,” said manager <b>Will Venable</b>. “He just continues to one-up himself and the honors just continue to roll in here. I’m just so proud of him.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/21/white-sox-tristan-peters-second-half-slump-all-star-game-brenton-doyle-davis-martin-kyle-teel-will-venable-derek-shomon-mets-luis-robert-jr" target="_blank" ><u>But Peters came out of the All-Star break in a 4-for-48 slump</u></a>, and slashing .320/.414/.640 in 27 games in August, alongside his sterling outfield defense, has affirmed that he’s no first-half fluke.</p><p>“It means a lot,” Peters said of the honor. “Getting back to sitting on my back side a little more, seeing the ball a little better. I think that helped a lot, just working with both hitting coaches.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">The AL Rookie of the Month <a href="https://t.co/QiMJmjha9D">pic.twitter.com/QiMJmjha9D</a></p>— James Fegan (@JRFegan) <a href="https://x.com/JRFegan/status/2095537590849925155?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 3, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>After hitting half of his 12 homers this year in August, Peters feels staying coiled on his back hip has allowed him to pull the ball in the air more frequently. While Venable noted that the Sox’ in-house projections liked Peters plenty when he was acquired in December, especially his defense, but his extra-base power has been a pleasant surprise.</p><p>He’s accessing it efficiently.</p><p>“I’ve been saying kind of as a joke, if you pull the ball you don’t need to hit it as hard,” said Peters.</p><h3><b>Night and day</b></h3><p>It’s rare to see a team taking batting practice on the field before any day game, let alone the finale of a seven-game road trip, as the White Sox did on Thursday.</p><p>Rather than a response to being shut out on just three hits on Wednesday, it’s part of the team trying to address an enormous split between their boffo offensive performance at night (.760 OPS), and paltry production in day games (.675 OPS).</p><p>“Trying to find solutions to play better during day games, which is something that we haven’t been doing a great job of,” Venable said. “Getting the boys fired up a little bit and a little bit of a different way, see if it has an impact and see if it leads to more runs for day games.”</p><h3><b>Teel nearing return?</b></h3><p><b>Kyle Teel</b> caught a full game on Wednesday night for the second time in his Triple-A rehab assignment for his left ankle sprain. The Sox manager’s demeanor did more to suggest his starting catcher will be activated this weekend than the full transcript might indicate.</p><p>“Close, he’s close,” Venable said.</p><h3><b>Hindsight is 20/20</b></h3><h3></h3><p>In the immediate wake of Wednesday’s 2-0 loss, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/02/playing-time-could-be-sparse-for-white-sox-right-handed-outfielders-down-the-stretch-randal-grichuk-will-venable-tommy-pham-brenton-doyle-luisangel-acuna-shane-smith-huascar-brazoban-mike-vasil-prelander-berroa-ky-bush" target="_blank" ><u>Venable defended not pinch-running for catcher </u><b><u>Drew Romo</u></b></a> by citing the importance of his defense. But when asked the next day if catchers are exempt for his typical eagerness to use substitutions, his self-assessment was more blunt.</p><p>“If you could do it all over again, I'm pinch-running for him,” Venable said. “You can call it a miss, a mess-up.”</p><h3><b>Pitching churn</b></h3><h3></h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/02/in-his-return-from-the-injured-list-davis-martin-looked-like-the-starting-pitcher-the-white-sox-need-brian-bannister-will-venable-zach-bove-houston-astros" target="_blank" ><u>With</u><b><u> Davis Martin</u></b><u> back in the rotation</u></a> and<b> Erick Fedde</b> scheduled to start on Friday, <b>Jose Urquidy</b> will move to long relief. Urquidy has a 4.58 ERA in 17 2/3 innings with the Sox, and his best work has been behind an opener.</p><p><b>Tyler Gilbert</b> cleared waivers after being designated for assignment on Tuesday, and was outrighted to Triple-A Charlotte.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Illinois sues ABC Plumbing, Heating, Cooling & Electric over alleged 'deceptive' practices
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul has filed a lawsuit against an Arlington Heights-based home repair company for alleged deceptive business practices that targeted seniors, according to court documents.</p><p>The lawsuit accuses ABC Plumbing, Heating, Cooling & Electric, Inc. of violating multiple state laws by having customers sign contracts for home repair work “at inflated prices by unlicensed technicians” that also waive the customers’ right to exit the contract, the office said in a statement.</p><p>The office is seeking a permanent injunction on the company’s work and a probe of all current contracts and monetary damages for customers who were allegedly harmed, the office said.</p><p>It’s also seeking the revocation, suspension, or forfeiture of the company’s licenses and other documents relating to its operations for home remodel and repair.</p><p>“ABC Plumbing, Heating, Cooling & Electric’s deceptive business practices are not only illegal but also disheartening because those practices target senior citizens,” Raoul said. “[Consumers] trust the company will present honest prices for complete work. Instead, ABC took advantage of its customers.”</p><p>ABC said it would "respond at the appropriate time," adding that it had not yet received the complaint or reviewed the allegations.</p><p>"For more than 70 years, ABC has served Chicago-area homeowners and earned their trust by operating with integrity," the company said in a statement to the Sun-Times.</p><p></p><p>The lawsuit alleges the company’s repair technicians engage in “upselling” by going to parts of customers’ homes they aren’t authorized to access, and present other issues as “emergencies, or even life-threatening hazards that require immediate remedy,” the office said. This includes showing them pictures and videos purported to be taken during the inspection that weren’t.</p><p>The customers, often senior citizens, are then presented with paperwork they usually aren’t allowed to read, the lawsuit says. The work is then completed by technicians who are unlicensed plumbers or specialists in other areas. And in some cases, an invoice was only created after a customer demanded to see one.</p><p>One woman, who was charged nearly $50,000 for sewage pipe replacement work that lasted several months and eventually led technicians to rip out portions of the wall in her basement, was told that the company doesn’t provide itemized lists of services provided, according to the suit.</p><p>She paid another company $1,500 to fix the work done by ABC after her basement continued flooding.</p><p>ABC eventually compensated her for the repairs, though she still is paying down a loan to cover the initial work, the lawsuit said. In other instances presented in the lawsuit, an elderly Schaumburg man was charged upwards of $6,000 for repairs he was never shown an invoice for.</p><p>James F. Coyne, Business Manager of the Chicago Plumbers Union, Local 130 UA, praised the lawsuit in a statement released by the attorney general's office.</p><p>“No homeowner should be taken advantage of when dealing with a plumbing emergency — especially the most vulnerable among us,” Coyne said. "Plumbers’ Local 130, UA, applauds Attorney General Kwame Raoul for enforcing the Illinois Plumbing License Law and protecting Illinois residents."</p>

entries.title: Tres líderes que trabajan con las comunidades inmigrantes de Chicago reflexionan sobre el impacto del Operativo Midway Blitz
entries.summary: <p>No salir de casa durante días o semanas. Estar siempre atento para protegerte a ti y a tus seres queridos. Esto puede conducir a un estado constante de miedo, estrés e incluso desesperanza.</p><p>En el último año, inmigrantes en muchas comunidades de Chicago y los suburbios han vivido esa montaña rusa de emociones mientras agentes federales de inmigración detuvieron a personas sin estatus migratorio legal y a otras que también fueron arrestadas en el marco de la campaña masiva de deportaciones del presidente Donald Trump.</p><p>No han sido los únicos en quedarse tambaleándose. Quienes tratan de ayudarlos también han sentido esto: líderes comunitarios, trabajadores sociales y personas que brindan servicios de salud mental a inmigrantes y sus familias.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-890000" name="module-890000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“El trauma secundario estaba tan generalizado", dice Mauricio Cifuentes, director de programas del Family Service and Mental Health Center de Cicero.</p><p>Muchos de esos ayudantes son inmigrantes, con historias de migración de sus propias familias a Estados Unidos. Estas son las historias de tres de ellos. Hablan de cómo el Operativo Midway Blitz los ha afectado y de lo que hacen para sobrellevarlo.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Cindy Eigler, directora ejecutiva de la Coalición para la Salud Mental de Inmigrantes, dice que libera su estrés boxeando.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>El boxeo como salvación</h3><h3></h3><p>En el apogeo del <a class="Link" href="http://suntimes.com/inmigracion" target="_blank" >Midway Blitz</a> en el otoño de 2025, Cindy Eigler abría su teléfono y veía cientos de mensajes en hilos de respuesta rápida que informaban sobre avistamientos de ICE y actividad en los suburbios del norte.</p><p>“Ocupaba todo mi espacio mental", dice Eigler, que vive en Evanston. “No dormía, y estaba muy gruñona con mis hijos y les respondía mal por cosas de las que no debía, y luego me sentía realmente impotente”.</p><p>Desde entonces ha mantenido un silbato junto a la puerta principal y en su auto porque respondía con regularidad a reportes de agentes del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE), a menudo en tiendas Home Depot y otros lugares donde se podían reunir migrantes. Era parte de su trabajo voluntario con un equipo de respuesta rápida que intentaba estar al tanto de los avistamientos de agentes.</p><p>También ayudó con las consecuencias de las acciones de inmigración, auxiliando a familias cuyos parientes fueron detenidos para conseguir ayuda para pagar la renta y la comida.</p><p>“Eso fue realmente pesado pero súper importante", dice Eigler.</p><p>Se sintió abrumada.</p><p>Todo su mundo —las 24 horas del día— fue consumido por el Operativo Midway Blitz. Era su trabajo voluntario y su trabajo diario.</p><p>Eigler es directora ejecutiva de la organización sin fines de lucro <a class="Link" href="https://www.ourcimh.org/" target="_blank" >Coalition for Immigrant Mental Health</a>. Una parte clave de su labor es prevenir crisis de salud mental creando espacios de sanación, mayormente virtuales, para inmigrantes, refugiados y trabajadores de primera línea de las organizaciones que los atienden, para ayudarlos a procesar lo que han visto y vivido.</p><p>Dice que intenta ayudar a la gente a entender qué es el trauma, cómo afecta su salud y cómo manejarlo.</p><p>Eigler solía trabajar con sobrevivientes de tortura policial. Así que dice que ya había escuchado historias horribles antes. Pero Midway Blitz se sintió distinto. Pegó cerca de casa.</p><p>Los padres de Eigler llegaron a Estados Unidos desde Venezuela cuando su madre estaba embarazada de ella. La familia de su padre eran refugiados que escaparon del Holocausto, y la familia de su madre tiene raíces en Egipto y Palestina.</p><p>Al crecer, la familia de Eigler no hablaba de dolor, rabia o tristeza.</p><p>“El trauma que han vivido y el no tener siempre es sentido de pertenencia o el ser marginados o discriminados, eso se refleja en cómo son y en cómo se mueven por el mundo", dice.</p><p>Cuenta que su madre lleva casi 50 años viviendo en Estados Unidos y, aun así, “le siguen diciendo todo el tiempo que se regrese de donde vino".</p><p>Eigler dice que antes intentaba contener sus sentimientos. Pero, durante la última década, ha encontrado una vía para soltarlos: el boxeo.</p><p>“Lo que me enseñaron desde pequeña fue: te aguantas, bajas la cabeza, ayudas a los demás y no dices lo que necesitas", dice. "El boxeo fue la primera vez en la que dije, ‘Oh, puedo realmente tener un deseo o una necesidad o un poder’".</p><p>Eigler sabía que las actualizaciones constantes en su hilo de respuesta rápida desencadenaban sentimientos de hipervigilancia. Le tomó alrededor de tres meses darse cuenta de que era demasiado. Se apartó del movimiento de respuesta rápida y, como resultado, pronto se sintió más presente como madre y en la coalición.</p><p>Ahora Eigler ha iniciado un programa para <a class="Link" href="https://www.ourcimh.org/community-resources" target="_blank" >integrar apoyo de salud mental</a> dentro de organizaciones comunitarias y ofrecer esa ayuda en lugares donde la gente ya se siente segura, entre quienes confían.</p><p>La coalición desarrolla programación con organizaciones socias y la diseña para responder a las necesidades particulares de cada comunidad, desde capacitación sobre estrés traumático secundario hasta arte o yoga. Hay <a class="Link" href="https://www.ourcimh.org/cimh-resources" target="_blank" >círculos de sanación</a> y espacios de escucha con el objetivo de ofrecer un lugar donde la gente pueda procesar libremente lo que carga y sentirse escuchada en comunidad.</p><p>Un año después del inicio de Midway Blitz, Eigler dice que aún está consumida y apasionada por su trabajo. Los inmigrantes siguen temiendo lo que podría pasarles a ellos y a sus familias. Piensa mucho en cómo asegurarse de que su salud mental sea una prioridad. Dice que el trauma puede desarrollarse a lo largo de generaciones.</p><p>“Tienes días buenos y días que se sienten más difíciles y en los que te sientes más pesimista y cínica sobre lo que está pasando", dice Eigler. “Me ayuda mucho estar en una organización donde puedo moverme con otras personas y tratar de apoyar en las formas que podemos y estar en acción”.</p><div class="Enhancement" </div><p></p><h3>Esperando ‘recobrar el rumbo’</h3><p>Angela Sedeño iba camino al banco en octubre pasado cuando supo que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/10/03/federal-agent-chemical-irritants-rico-fresh-logan-square" target="_blank" >habían lanzado gas lacrimógeno</a> afuera de Rico Fresh Market en Logan Square, frente al Centro de Esperanza LoSAH, la clínica bilingüe de salud mental donde es directora ejecutiva.</p><p>Vio a gente correr en busca de refugio. Corrió a revisar a sus vecinas y vecinos. Todavía no puede quitarse de la cabeza la imagen de dos de sus empleadas más jóvenes entrando con los ojos llorosos y enrojecidos por el gas y cómo se sintió de que no pudo protegerlas.</p><p>“Fueron cosas para las que no estábamos preparados, que no podíamos haber previsto", dice Sedeño. “Tenemos todos estos planes de emergencia y de crisis para todo tipo de cosas, como crisis de salud mental, pero ciertamente no para que usen ese tipo de tácticas en la calle".</p><p>El centro LoSAH es una clínica financiada por la comunidad que ofrece servicios de salud mental asequibles en inglés y español en los vecindarios de Logan Square, Avondale y Hermosa, incluyendo terapia, grupos de apoyo y prácticas colectivas de sanación como baños de sonido y círculos de tambor.</p><p>El rol de Sedeño abarca desde formar alianzas comunitarias y supervisar los servicios clínicos hasta proporcionar intervenciones comunitarias y tratar de estar al tanto de las necesidades de salud mental de la comunidad.</p><p>La responsabilidad de atender a los clientes del centro y también a su personal puede ser mucha incluso en tiempos ordinarios. Pero la incertidumbre y la violencia de Midway Blitz afectaron a sus empleados, la mitad de ellos biculturales y bilingües, mientras atendían a clientes que experimentaban pánico, miedo y desesperación, al mismo tiempo que navegaban sus propios sentimientos de rabia e impotencia.</p><p>Sedeño dice que trata de asegurarse de que sus empleados tomen descansos y no se sobrecarguen. Usa una práctica llamada supervisión reflexiva para crear espacios donde las personas puedan compartir y procesar sus sentimientos con la ayuda de supervisores capacitados.</p><p>“Todo lo que haríamos por un cliente, también lo hacemos por nuestro personal", dice Sedeño, una mexicoamericana de primera generación.</p><p>“Crecer siendo de piel morena en Estados Unidos significó que, en distintos momentos de mi infancia, había discriminación por color de piel, por el idioma", dice Sedeño. “Y entonces, ver todo esto sucediendo tan descaradamente, parte el corazón. Me parte el corazón escuchar las historias y ver las caras que se parecen a la tuya siendo señaladas".</p><p>Para cuidarse a sí misma, se apoya en una terapeuta, en su familia, en su fe y en las muchas organizaciones aliadas del centro LoSAH.</p><p>Con el inicio del nuevo año escolar y la incertidumbre que esto puede traer, Sedeño y su equipo se preparan para apoyar a las familias a medida que sus miedos, ansiedades y traumas resurjan.</p><p>“Esperaría que en algún momento recobremos el rumbo y la gente tenga la oportunidad de descansar y recuperarse porque eso aún no ha ocurrido", dice Sedeño.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-895ffd" name="image-895ffd"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Vero Ortiz, directora principal de bienestar comunitario de la organización sin fines de lucro Enlace Chicago en La Villita.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Devolver la calma y la esperanza</h3><p>La Villita, el vecindario del suroeste predominantemente mexicano, estuvo en el centro de los operativos de control migratorio el otoño pasado. Helicópteros zumbando y silbatos advirtiendo que había agentes de inmigración cerca se convirtieron en la norma.</p><p>Vero Ortiz, directora principal de bienestar comunitario de la organización sin fines de lucro Enlace Chicago, lo recuerda así: “Hubo días en los que no veías a nadie en las calles. Había tanto miedo. Y ahora vivimos en el centro de ese miedo".</p><p>Aunque ahora hay menos agentes por las calles y la aplicación de la ley de inmigración se ha vuelto más selectiva, Ortiz dice que el impacto psicológico persiste.</p><p>Ortiz vive en los suburbios y ha trabajado en Enlace durante dos años, pero se identifica como alguien “adoptada por La Villita”. Como mexicoamericana de primera generación, Ortiz habla de tener una fuerte conexión cultural con el barrio, por lo que tener que luchar contra un sistema que, dice, intenta borrar a la comunidad vibrante, ha provocado dolor, rabia y estrés.</p><p>“Lloré esta mañana", dice Ortiz. “Vi una publicación de una niña pequeña parada entre un agente de ICE y su mamá. Sigue pasando".</p><p>Sin embargo, las emociones intensas de Ortiz no han frenado su trabajo. Al contrario, lo alimentan, con el impulso de ofrecer más opciones preventivas para empoderar a las y los residentes y prepararlos para la próxima crisis.</p><p>Ortiz ha estado trabajando para atender el aumento en la demanda de servicios de salud mental. Consiguió financiamiento municipal este año para una terapeuta comunitaria adicional y una terapeuta escolar, así como para una nueva especialista en apoyo familiar que pueda ayudar a personas que, por ejemplo, aún podrían tener miedo de salir de sus casas.</p><p>“A veces podemos trabajar a cien millas por hora aunque, como líderes, no pedimos a nuestro personal que lo haga", dice Ortiz, que ha trabajado en bienestar infantil e intervención con pandillas. “Creo que lo hacen porque aman lo que hacen. Así que también es mi responsabilidad decirles, ‘Oigan, les voy a pedir que no se agoten’ porque necesito que mi personal esté bien para que podamos servir a la comunidad”.</p><p><i>Contribuyó: Feixu Chen </i></p><p><i>Mary Ellen Ritter y Navya Shukla produjeron este reportaje como parte del Medill Investigative Lab–Chicago de Northwestern University. </i></p><p><i>Este reportaje se produjo como parte de la</i> <a class="Link" href="https://mentalhealthjournalism.org/parity-collaborative/" target="_blank" ><i>Mental Health Parity Collaborative</i></a><i>, un grupo de salas de redacción y universidades que cubre el acceso y las desigualdades en la atención de salud mental en Estados Unidos. </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Bears need health, production from WR Rome Odunze to form dynamic duo
entries.summary: <p>For all the concern about Rome Odunze’s right foot — he declared in June that he was facing a “new normal” after missing five games last season last year with a stress fracture — the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> wide receiver made it through the summer just fine.</p><p>Until Thursday.</p><p>He left after the walk-through period of the team’s last practice before a three-day break. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/03/bears-practice-report-rb-dandre-swift-wr-rome-odunze-leave-with-injuries" target="_blank" >Odunze</a> seemed to be favoring his right foot after a misstep. Odunze wanted to remain in practice, but was escorted off by a trainer. A source said that the move appeared to be precautionary and that early indications were positive.</p><p>"It’s an adjustment," receiver Kalif Raymond said afterward. "But, also, we’re praying that he’s OK."</p><p>The Bears won’t return to Halas Hall until they hold a light practice Monday. On Tuesday — the next day coach Ben Johnson is scheduled to talk to the media — the team will hold a more strenuous practice. The Bears don’t owe the NFL its first injury report of the season until Wednesday. Until then, though, another injury is the last thing the Bears — or Odunze — needs. In 12 games last season, he had 661 receiving yards on 44 catches, a step back from his rookie season.</p><p>The Bears need Odunze to be productive — and healthy — this year. They went into the offseason with one of the league’s most intriguing wide receiver trios — and quickly turned it into a duo. Their decision to trade DJ Moore to the Bills opened up salary cap space in 2026 and into the future, when the Bears hope they have to pay Caleb Williams like a franchise quarterback. It also put the onus on Odunze and Luther Burden to perform like one of the best receiver pairings in the NFL.</p><p>The Bears would be thrilled if they were merely the best in the NFC North.</p><p>The bar in the division, though, is sky high.</p><p>No wide receiver duo in the NFL was better last year than the Lions’ Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams, who combined for 2,518 receiving yards and 18 touchdowns last year. The Vikings boast perennial superstar Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison, who combined for 126 catches, 1,658 yards and five scores.</p><p>Odunze and Burden were far off their pace, catching 91 passes for 1,313 yards and eight touchdowns.</p><p>Johnson’s passing attack will undoubtedly feature tight ends Colston Loveland — the Bears’ leading receiver last year — and Cole Kmet. Running back D’Andre Swift has caught more than three passes per game during his career. Newcomers Zavion Walker and Raymond will be part of the Bears’ speed packages, and Jahdae Walker will look to build on his strong finish to last year.</p><p>If the Bears are going to be dynamic, though, it has to come from their top wide receiver duo.</p><p>Odunze and Burden had drastically different training camps. Odunze spent camp looking like the player who had five touchdown catches over the first four games last year. Burden came in with more buzz than any other Bears player — Johnson notoriously said he’d buy stock in the second-year receiver if he could — before hurting his groin when he went up for a contested catch against Tyrique Stevenson on Aug. 8. He returned to full practice status just this week and is expected to be ready for the season opener Sept. 13 in Carolina.</p><p>Ben Johnson called Odunze, the ninth pick of the 2024 draft, “Mr. Consistency” during training camp. When Johnson called a run play against the Titans during joint practice last week, Odunze nailed a safety on a crackback block. His coach positively levitated.</p><p>“That inspires me to, not <i>want</i> to get him the football,” Johnson said. “But I <i>need</i> to get him the football when I see things like that. …</p><p>“He's doing all the little things, the things that maybe other people don't notice and the coaching staff is very appreciative of, because it's going to help us win games. He's going to be a key cog in what we do.”</p><p>Their playing styles are different. The Bears want Odunze to be a deep threat who catches the ball at the highest point possible.</p><p>“Being able to stretch the field vertically … “ quarterback Caleb Williams said. “One-on-one opportunities creates more of an advantage for us. That’s what we’re trying to figure out and find.”</p><p>They want Burden to get the ball in his hands and then do damage — last year, he finished third among qualifying receivers in yards after catch per reception.</p><p>Odunze spent training camp trying to master some of what made Burden so good — and vice versa.</p><p>“I feel like my route running is up there, but I have a few [things] that I can clear up and make even better,” Odunze said recently. “Yards after catch — run after catch — is definitely something I'm looking to improve on as well. I'm watching Luther's tape, looking at how he's making defenders miss.”</p><p>Burden has high expectations for himself, too.</p><p>“I expect to have a good explosive year. …” he said last month. “High explosive plays. Making people miss. Scoring touchdowns. Winning games.”</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: White Sox remain confident in Luis Castillo and Munetaka Murakami despite ugly road trip performance
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON — If there was a theme of Luis Castillo’s previous three starts, other than ineffectiveness, it was struggling to establish his four-seam fastball at the top of the zone.</p><p>In outings against the Cubs and Twins, Castillo gave up first-inning homers on fastballs that stayed hittably thigh-high. By the time he found the feel on locating heaters elevated enough to set up the rest of his arsenal, the opportunity for a respectable line score was already gone.</p><p>“There’s some delivery stuff that goes along with that,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> pitching coach Zach Bove told the Sun-Times. “But that's what he needs to do, that's what sets up the arsenal as far as the slider and changeup working off that.”</p><p>In that vein, Astros star Jose Altuve opening up the scoring Thursday against Castillo with a first-inning two-run homer on a helmet-high fastball felt like the Sox right-hander getting punished for doing what he’s supposed to do.</p><p>Instead, the bloodletting that followed in a 6-2 defeat to clinch a losing road trip — the fifth time in Castillo’s six starts with the White Sox where he’s allowed four runs or more and lasted fewer than five innings — suggested there are no simple solutions to what’s ailing their prized trade-deadline acquisition.</p><p>“I would like to know why,” Castillo said of his struggles via interpreter. “That is something that I’m still trying to figure out.”</p><p>At least, not solutions like yanking Castillo out of the rotation after a 7.52 ERA in six starts.</p><p>“We believe in him,” manager Will Venable said postgame. “I just had a conversation with him just to reaffirm that.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Will Venable on Luis Castillo <a href="https://t.co/OT54Lzzf5p">pic.twitter.com/OT54Lzzf5p</a></p>— James Fegan (@JRFegan) <a href="https://x.com/JRFegan/status/2095619700059161012?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 3, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>With better luck, Castillo’s worst results to date in a Sox uniform — 4 IP, 6 ER–could have been somewhat better. Isaac Paredes’ RBI double in a four-run Astros’ third is a deep, but routine fly out in most MLB stadiums. Daulton Varsho’s two-run triple was set up by misfired fastballs, but came on a slider well below the zone. Christian Walker’s RBI single to plate Varsho was one of the softest hit balls of the afternoon.</p><p>But these are all possible when the 33-year-old Castillo, once a preeminent strikeout artist, is not missing bats. Castillo had a career-low 19.4% strikeout rate when he was acquired on Aug. 2, and has struck out 18.4% of hitters in a Sox uniform. Castillo says he feels good physically, but his velocity was down a tick, to approximately 94 mph, for the second-straight start.</p><p>It’s far-fetched that Castillo is done being an effective major league starter. But it also is unlikely that a turnaround from season-long struggles, over three weeks that could dictate the winner of the American League Central, is imminent.</p><p>With 22 games left, Venable says he’ll be managing like it’s the playoffs in the final stretch, meaning openers used in front of Castillo and others. But the Sox simultaneously seem content to dance with who they brought, an approach that extends to ideas of sliding a slumping Munetaka Murakami down in the lineup after a 3-for-24, 12-strikeout showing on this road trip.</p><p>“There have been at-bats where I’ve been thinking too much about getting the angles too much higher on the swings,” Murakami said via interpreter. “Even on the normal outs, I’ve been a little bit negative on the mental side, about even if I have a good at-bat and it’s an out, I’ve been a bit negative. It’s important for me to think in a positive way.”</p><p>Even with their deadline additions not providing a boost, there is stuff for the Sox to be positive about. They remain up three games in the AL Central, they return home this weekend to a soft slate of opponents. They control their playoff destiny to an enviable degree, even if it feels like they’re waiting to play like the team they’ve flashed signs of being.</p><p>“One trigger, one little key,” Murakami said via interpreter. “It’s about finding that one little thing and moving on forward so I can get back on track.”</p><p></p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true"
