entries.title: Trump again appeals to Supreme Court on mail-voting restrictions as midterm elections loom
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON — The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court Thursday to reject an order by a federal judge that halts it from implementing a new rule regulating mail ballots, hours after being unable to tell that judge whether the computer system that would govern the entire project was operational yet.</p><p>The administration filed its appeal the afternoon before mail ballots were scheduled to be sent out by North Carolina, which on Friday kicks off a wave of states shipping ballots out for the rapidly approaching <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/midterm-election-messaging-economy-trump-socialists-prices-dc7a63a6f455fa35d207a543b64c4706" target="_blank" >midterm election</a>. Its appeal was part of a flurry of last-minute litigation as the federal government struggles to implement President Donald Trump's <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/donald-trump-mail-voting-elections-47cc334b1fb7742244a9c4f176b355cd" target="_blank" >restrictions on mail ballots</a> before the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/midterm-election-messaging-economy-trump-socialists-prices-dc7a63a6f455fa35d207a543b64c4706" target="_blank" >midterm elections</a> in November, and came even as legal wrangling over Trump’s executive order continued in lower courts.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-mail-voting-supreme-court-157afc3c195ce0a62c522da5ce904b04" target="_blank" >The high court’s conservative majority previously allowed the president’s plan</a> to move ahead, but it has not decided whether the plan is legal.</p><p>Under Trump’s executive order, the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/postal-service-midterms-trump-mail-voting-b4b9ef095b4d6bceab18adbb34814640" target="_blank" >U.S. Postal Service</a> could refuse to deliver ballots from states that do not follow a uniform envelope style and submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal that was apparently still inactive Thursday.</p><p>During a hearing in Boston, U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani repeatedly questioned Justice Department attorney Michael Velchik about whether the Postal Service could actually implement Trump's plan from an executive order he issued last spring. The key piece is the online portal, which would track tens of millions of mail ballots. States would be required to upload their list of mail voters to the portal to have ballots delivered, and if the data there didn't match what was on the envelopes, the ballots would not be sent.</p><h3>Unclear if key system has been set up</h3><p>“I don’t even have a declaration from the Postal Service: ‘This is how it will work.’ I don’t have it. I have nothing,” Talwani said, adding later that it felt like the government was running an “experiment” to see if the system would work in the upcoming election.</p><p>“As you sit here today, you can’t tell me the government has a program ready to go?” Talwani asked.</p><p>Velchik repeated that the Postal Service would “fully implement the rule” that it published last month, triggering the latest round of litigation. He argued the main issue is whether Talwani has the legal power to stop it.</p><p>“The $64,000 question is: Is this authorized by the statute?” Velchik said.</p><p>Talwani is considering whether to <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-executive-order-elections-midterms-voting-rights-159c192e48670a8740a6a378c683cb61" target="_blank" >extend her temporary order barring the Postal Service</a> from requiring use of the system through Sept. 10. The first state to send out all its mail ballots, North Carolina, is scheduled to begin shipping them out Friday, with other states quickly following.</p><p>Talwani has been here before. In June, she <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-executive-order-elections-mail-voting-b28c3425c1dc968cd0f57c61fb7a684e" target="_blank" >prohibited the administration</a> from implementing Trump's executive order for the November election, ruling the changes came too close to voting for the federal government to embark on such a project.</p><p>But the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-mail-voting-supreme-court-157afc3c195ce0a62c522da5ce904b04" target="_blank" >Supreme Court</a> late last month ruled that Talwani's order was premature because the Postal Service had not yet published regulations governing how it would apply Trump's order. <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/postal-service-midterms-trump-mail-voting-b4b9ef095b4d6bceab18adbb34814640" target="_blank" >The agency did so</a> just before the high court ruling came down, prompting Democrats and voting rights groups to swiftly refile their lawsuits.</p><p>They counter that the president has no authority to set election rules, which is a power designated by the Constitution to the states, and in some cases, to Congress.</p><h3><b>Tangled legal fight goes up to election deadlines</b></h3><p>They won an initial victory with Talwani's 14-day restraining order. In a sign of the pressures on the administration, its lawyers already <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-voting-mail-ballots-midterms-executive-order-8ef4a669a50f3406481ffb8387ccad3c" target="_blank" >appealed</a> that order to the 1st Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston, but they added the Supreme Court appeal Thursday and urged the top justices to act quickly.</p><p>Trump has <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/f0a5b003db26dbb19778bcdcb45f9a3f" target="_blank" >long opposed mail voting</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/virus-outbreak-joe-biden-election-2020-donald-trump-elections-3e8170c3348ce3719d4bc7182146b582" target="_blank" >falsely blamed it</a> for his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden, even though he often <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/donald-trump-vote-by-mail-bd52fd205f4484237d5b77d2e7319350" target="_blank" >uses that method</a> to cast his own ballot.</p><p>Election officials say there's simply no way they can comply with the Postal Service directives, which could require a complete overhaul of their operations. Before it delivers mail ballots for any state, the Postal Service would have to approve the design of the envelopes that contain them and have the state upload a list of voters receiving them to <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/midterm-elections-postal-service-mail-voting-7f7cf4fdf2e9cf369ae96f96fbda03f2" target="_blank" >an online portal</a>.</p><p>Some ballots have already gone out. A few municipalities in Wisconsin opted to send mail ballots to voters earlier this week, but Friday marks the full kickoff of voting as North Carolina starts shipping its mail ballots to all voters who requested them.</p><p>The administration has contended the changes are relatively minor and legal.</p><p>“While the States have primary authority to regulate the manner of elections, they cannot choose to use the federal mails to carry out their elections but then insist that their election-related mail is somehow exempt from the Postal Service’s rulemaking authority, conferred by Congress, to regulate envelope design and addressee information,” Trump's solicitor general, John Sauer, wrote in the appeal.</p><h3><b>No red states have said they’ll use system</b></h3><p>Still, the hearing before Talwani focused more on practicalities — especially that the portal was still not active, while most election offices have already printed their envelopes and ballots.</p><p>Velchik told the judge that the federal government is offering states the choice to opt into the system, but the Postal Service has yet to identify a single state that has done so. None of the 12 states that intervened in the lawsuit to argue the Trump administration has the right to require the program have announced that they have voluntarily opted into it.</p><p>Talwani scolded Missouri Solicitor General Lou Capozzi for arguing on behalf of the project.</p><p>“You want the voters in your states to be disenfranchised,” Talwani said. “I don't understand the interest.”</p><p>Capozzi said that was misinformation: “There is no risk that people would be disenfranchised.”</p><p>A whistleblower report made public this week warns that the postal system's requirements could lead to millions of mail ballots <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/midterm-elections-postal-service-mail-voting-7f7cf4fdf2e9cf369ae96f96fbda03f2" target="_blank" >never being sent.</a> The new rule requires all ballots to be physically brought to post offices before being mailed to voters. But if a single one's bar code registers an error, the whole batch gets thrown out, even if it contains tens of thousands of legitimate ballots.</p>

entries.title: Previewing Week 3's top high school football games
entries.summary: <p>It’s a loaded weekend around the area in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/09/03/high-school-football-scores-chicago-illinois" >Week 3</a>. Here are previews of a few of the best games.</p><h3>No. 3 Lincoln-Way East at No. 10 Homewood-Flossmoor, 7:30 p.m. Friday</h3><p>H-F (2-0) has been one of the breakout teams in the early going, stunning Bolingbrook 31-0 and blanking Richards 35-0 in the first two weeks. Robert Williams III returned an interception for a touchdown against Richards and Wisconsin commit David Hill anchors a dominant defensive line. Rahsaan Coleman threw a pair of touchdown passes to lead the H-F offense. Lincoln-Way East (2-0) doesn't have the Power Four talent of recent years, apart from Illinois-bound offensive lineman Mason Halliman. But quarterback Evan LeFevour and running back Aidan Cavanaugh lead a grind-it-out offense.</p><h3>No. 8 St. Rita at No. 1 Loyola, 7 p.m. Friday</h3><h3></h3><p>This shapes up as the first serious local test for Loyola (2-0), which blanked Warren in Week 1 and beat Indianapolis Cathedral 33-19 last week. Junior quarterback Matthew Lee passed for three touchdowns — two to Charlie Fowler — and ran for another against Cathedral as Loyola rallied from a 13-7 halftime deficit. St. Rita (1-1) is coming off a wild 36-35 win at Glenbard West after getting the decisive two-point conversion with 42 seconds left. Lindenwood commit Brandon Johnson Jr. ran for 154 yards and three touchdowns for the Mustangs, while quarterback John Fennell had 282 total yards and a TD.</p><h3>No. 17 Nazareth at No. 2 Mount Carmel, 7:30 Friday</h3><h3></h3><p>Mount Carmel (1-1) has already played two of the wildest games of the season, allowing the last 28 points in a 42-23 loss to East St. Louis and then rallying 30 points down to beat St. Joseph Regional (N.J.) 48-44 on ESPN last week. Plainfield East transfer Brady Cloherty led the comeback, passing for 309 yards and a program-record seven touchdowns, including five to the receiving duo of Quentin Burrell (Michigan) and Marshaun Thornton. Nazareth (1-1) bounced back from an opening loss to IC Catholic with an impressive 27-3 victory against York. North Dakota commit Charles Calhoun ran for a pair of scores to lead the Roadrunners.</p><h3>No. 15 St. Francis at No. 6 Brother Rice, 7 p.m. Friday</h3><h3></h3><p>This is a matchup of returning state champs off to 1-1 starts. Reigning 7A winner Brother Rice was hurt by penalties in a 22-21 Week 1 loss to Lincoln-Way East before rolling past outmanned Woodlawn last week. Freshman quarterback Sam Holcomb, who has split time with senior Rocco Galasso, already has accounted for eight touchdowns. Notre Dame-bound Brayden Parks and Kameron McGee, one of the nation's top juniors, are the leaders of one of the state's premier defensive lines. Returning 5A champ St. Francis lost on the road as New Palestine (Ind.) in Week 1 before cruising past Clemente last week. Tivias Caldwell Jr. is a productive running back who had 182 all-purpose yards in the opener.</p><h3>No. 24 St. Charles North at No. 16 Geneva, 7 p.m. Friday</h3><p>Geneva (1-1) is coming off a 44-42 loss to returning 8A runner-up Oswego in which quarterback Ben Peterson (Eastern Michigan) passed for 443 yards and five touchdowns. State sprint champ Bennett Konkey (Illinois) had 10 catches for 217 yards and four TDs. St. Charles North is 2-0 after dominant wins over 8A opponents Minooka and South Elgin. The North Stars have had good results using a pair of quarterbacks in Landon Conroy and Dashel Von Qualen along with running back Tommy Vendl.</p>

entries.title: With Ben Brown out for season, Cubs focus on current arms rather than count on rehabbing possibilities
entries.summary: <p>After experiencing a setback in his quest to return to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> this season, right-hander Ben Brown is done for the year.</p><p>Manager Craig Counsell said Thursday that Brown, who was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/24/cubs-injuries-pitching-rotation-ben-brown-edward-cabrera-injured-list-matthew-boyd-jameson-taillon-cade-horton-craig-counsell-jed-hoyer-justin-steele" target="_blank" >sidelined in June</a> by a stress fracture in a vertebra in his neck, won’t pitch again this season, snuffing out any hopes he could step in as a relief option down the stretch and in the postseason.</p><p>Reports about Brown’s rehab had been nothing but positive until <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/26/cubs-ben-brown-injury-setback-neck-fracture-playoff-bullpen-2027-starting-rotation" target="_blank" >he experienced symptoms</a> during a live batting-practice session last week in Arizona.</p><p>Now the Cubs are forced to look to next season when it comes to a guy who was, when healthy, among the most effective pitchers in the majors earlier this season, posting a 1.70 ERA in eight starts.</p><p>‘‘After consulting with doctors, it’s just [that he needs] more rest,’’ Counsell said. ‘‘There’s healing but not enough to allow the discomfort to go away. So we need to spend more time healing.</p><p>‘‘The bone, it’s healing, but you can still see signs of an injury. The original thing was, ‘We’re going to rest for a bit, and then we’re going to go when we’re not re-creating symptoms.’ It worked until [last week].’’</p><p>Brown was among a group of rehabbing pitchers who might have given the Cubs an embarrassment of intriguing options come October — a group getting more attention in the middle of the rough patch the bullpen is enduring right now.</p><p>But the Cubs’ brass has been cautious about the idea of left-hander Justin Steele getting back to the big leagues this season, given that he has missed the vast majority of the last two campaigns while recovering from elbow surgery.</p><p>Right-hander Edward Cabrera has been dogged by blister issues this season and hasn’t been very effective when healthy.</p><p>Reliever Shelby Miller (Tommy John surgery) was signed with little expectation he would be available this season, though Counsell on Thursday described him and Cabrera as ‘‘the two guys who are closest.’’</p><p>Given how effective Brown was this season, he was arguably the most likely to make an impact. Now he’ll be part of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/20/cade-townsend-is-cubs-pitchings-far-future-but-whats-near-future-look-like-when-starters-hit-free-agency" target="_blank" >the large number of question marks about the starting rotation</a> in 2027 and beyond.</p><p>The stress fracture was discovered — two years after the fact — to be the injury that ended Brown’s season early in 2024, then misdiagnosed as an osteoma. Brown called that clarity a blessing and said he saw a clearer path forward in June than he did two years ago, when the Cubs spent so much time trying to figure out what was bothering him.</p><p>He also said he would put in long-term work on figuring out what changes he could make that might prevent this from happening in the future. Whether that’s possible remains to be seen.</p><p>‘‘When you’re talking about those kinds of mechanics, some of those things are innate or how your body moves or reacts to pitching,’’ team president Jed Hoyer said Tuesday. ‘‘I’m not saying he can’t do it, but it’s more challenging than retraining your arm path or something like that. It’s something physical that we have to figure out.’’</p><p>‘‘These guys throw hard because their body moves a certain way,’’ Counsell said. ‘‘You can’t invent another way to do that.’’</p><p>Meanwhile, Counsell & Co. are focused on the relievers they have at their disposal, several of whom are struggling right now.</p><p>The Cubs might have dodged a significant blow after closer Jacob Webb <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/02/cubs-brewers-jacob-misiorowski-jacob-webb-injury-bullpen-nl-central-standings" target="_blank" >took a line drive off his right (throwing) arm</a>, with Counsell saying the Cubs are hopeful he won’t have to go on the injured list.</p><p>But Webb and fellow high-leverage reliever Daniel Palencia keep giving up runs.</p><p>‘‘The bullpen is a ‘today’ question, so we’re worried about the guys we’ve got right now,’’ Counsell said. ‘‘Those [rehabbing] guys have jobs to do, and that’s to continue pitching.</p><p>‘‘They’re coming off injuries. I think they have to answer health questions still and recovery questions still. Those are different questions than the guys here.’’</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Cardinal Cupich, nuns challenge ‘right-to-die’ law, say Illinois ‘has no business’ forcing assisted suicide
entries.summary: <p>Cardinal Blase Cupich has added his high-profile name to a federal lawsuit challenging Illinois' assisted suicide law, arguing that the practice is unconstitutional and "denies the choice of a dignified death" to Catholics who want to die naturally. </p><p>Cupich's suit is one of at least three filed ahead of the law's effective date: Sept. 12. A federal judge is expected to rule Friday on a request for a preliminary injunction on one of the suits. Cupich joined two orders of nuns and an Illinois pharmacist Thursday in seeking to block the law via a permanent injunction. </p><p>Illinois joined 11 other states that have passed so-called <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2025/11/03/illinois-right-to-die-bill-pritzker" target="_blank" >“right-to-die” legislation<u>,</u></a> which is opposed by many religious leaders and disability rights activists.</p><p>"Where the current Pope, along with Cardinal Cupich, has commanded that Illinois Catholics must 'respect the sacredness of life from the very beginning to the very end' by not participating in assisted suicide, the state has no business forcing them to do just that," states the suit, filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois. </p><p>Cupich, who leads the Archdiocese of Chicago, was among those who vocally opposed the law last year and accused Gov. JB Pritzker of putting "Illinois on a dangerous and heartbreaking path — one that legitimizes suicide as a valid solution for life’s challenges."</p><p>The plaintiffs state they want a federal judge to stop the state from providing counsel and information about assisted suicide — and from helping a patient qualify or fill a prescription for "suicide drugs," among other requests. </p><p>The law at issue was signed by Pritzker in December 2025 and will allow people 18 or older to request a fatal medication if they’ve been diagnosed by two physicians with an illness that will result in death within six months. Patients will have to make a series of oral and written requests themselves — not through a guardian, surrogate, advance legal document or other proxy — with witnesses attesting.</p><p>Physicians will have to confirm the patient is “of sound mind” and inform them of other end-of-life options such as hospice and palliative care. And if prescribed a life-ending drug, patients would administer it themselves. Healthcare providers aren’t required to participate.</p><p>Despite that opt-out process, the plaintiffs say the law is unconstitutional, in part because the First Amendment "requires the government to respect and stay out of matters of governance within religious institutions." The suit states the Constitution's protection of the free exercise of religion prohibits the government "from burdening the sincere religious beliefs of Plaintiffs and the patients they serve" and also prohibits the government from enacting legal burdens that fall on religious adherents. </p><p>It also claims the Constitution's protections against compelled speech prevent the government from forcing Catholic doctors and nurses "to speak the government's preferred, supportive message of assisted suicide." And it states the law violates the Americans with Disabilities Act, the equal protection clause and the supremacy clause. Another one of the three suits also claims the law discriminates against people with disabilities by not providing them with sufficient protections against abuse of the practice.</p><p>"In passing the Act, Illinois has stripped that very choice away from the Sisters and their patients — denying the choice of a dignified death to the many residents of Illinois who, following their sincere religious beliefs, wish to die naturally in the Sisters' faith-filled homes, secure in the knowledge that they will not be urged to consider cutting short their life through suicide," the suit states. </p><p>The suit also takes issue with medical providers having to inform and counsel patients about their options — although the law specifies that providers provide that information only if a patient requests end-of-life medications. And it points out that physicians, mental health professionals and pharmacists will have to participate in a multistep process should patients choose end-of-life drugs. </p><p>It also claims allowing patients to die by suicide will jeopardize their federal healthcare funding, like Medicare and Medicaid — although federal law already prohibits federal taxpayer money from being used to fund or administer the practice.</p><p>Plaintiffs include the Carmelite Sisters for the Aged and Infirm's St. Patrick's Residence; Little Sisters of the Poor, Chicago Province; Little Sisters of the Poor — Palatine; Cupich; Luke Vander Bleek, a Catholic pharmacist from Morrison and Fitzgerald Pharmacy, a pharmacy in Morrison. The suit's defendants are Illinois Department of Veterans Affairs Director Terry Prince; Illinois Department of Public Health Director Sameer Vohra and Mario Treto Jr., secretary of the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation. </p><p>The Illinois attorney general's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.</p>

entries.title: Bears practice report: RB D'Andre Swift, WR Rome Odunze leave with injuries
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ Thursday practice:</p><h3><b>Concerns arise</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Bears running back D’Andre Swift, who had been impeccably healthy in training camp, left late in practice with an apparent left leg injury. Wide receiver Rome Odunze got hurt, too, and left in the first half of practice with what looked like a right leg injury. Odunze had a stress fracture in his right foot most of last season.</p><p>At running back, the Bears already are down backup Kyle Monangai (knee), and coach Ben Johnson said Tuesday he is week-to-week.</p><h3><b>Dress rehearsal</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The team went a little over two hours, but took a 10-minute break in the air-conditioned Walter Payton Center in the middle of it to simulate halftime. They did that with the Titans last week as well.</p><h3><b>Booker back</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Defensive end Austin Booker was out the past week or so with a groin injury, but was full-go in practice Wednesday. He was running with the first team and doing all drills.</p><h3><b>Just in case</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The Bears spent a few minutes of practice working on the rare scenario of a fair catch and free kick. That comes up less than once a season, but it allows a team to try a field goal without any opposing rush, and kicker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/23/cairo-santos-is-the-best-kicker-in-bears-history-in-year-13-he-thinks-hell-be-even-better" >Cairo Santos</a> made it comfortably from about 58 yards.</p><h3><b>Waiting for Turner</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Bears defensive lineman Shemar Turner was at practice in full uniform, but watched from the side. Turner tore his ACL in Week 8 last season and is on the physically unable-to-perform list to start this one, meaning he’ll miss at least the first four games.</p><h3><b>What’s next?</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Players get the weekend off before diving into preparation for the Panthers on Monday.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Review of ex-NFL reporter Dianna Russini's work at the Athletic concludes she didn't comply with standards
entries.summary: <p>An investigation by The Athletic has concluded that former NFL reporter Dianna Russini violated the company's standards because of her relationship with New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel that led to her resignation in April.</p><p>The report drew no conclusions about the nature of Russini's relationship with Vrabel, who said he took accountability for his actions without addressing photos released of the coach and the reporter at a resort in Arizona. He stepped away from the team on the third day of the NFL draft to begin counseling and returned soon afterward.</p><p>"We neither completed an investigation nor reached any conclusion about the nature of the full relationship between Vrabel and Russini, but the totality of the public photographs are enough to conclude a violation of company policy," the report said.</p><p>Steven Ginsberg, executive editor at The Athletic, a New York Times-owned sports outlet, addressed the report in a message to employees Thursday.</p><p>"We undertook this review to ensure the integrity of our journalism and to maintain the trust our audience places in us. Nothing is more important than our credibility," Ginsberg wrote.</p><p>Mike Semel, editorial director for standards and quality at The Athletic, conducted the review of Russini's work, examining 903 stories, 204 episodes of her podcast and 77 videos.</p><p>"The review found that the vast majority of Dianna's stories were unrelated to Vrabel, and most of those that mentioned him did not raise concerns," Ginsberg told the staff. "We have, however, added editor's notes to four stories — one written and three videos — that did not meet our standards."</p><p>The photos of Vrabel and Russini were taken in Sedona, Arizona, before the annual NFL meetings that began in Phoenix on March 29, according to the New York Post. Vrabel and Russini are both married. The NFL did not investigate Vrabel's actions.</p><p>"Russini's relationship with Vrabel was in clear violation of The Athletic's standards," Semel wrote in the report. "Regardless of whether the relationship was romantic, it was a breach and should have been disclosed."</p><p>Vrabel led the Patriots to the Super Bowl in February, where they lost to Seattle. He was the AP NFL Coach of the Year in his first season in New England, finishing 63 points ahead of Jacksonville's Liam Coen.</p><p>Russini told the AP on Thursday that she stands by what she wrote in her resignation letter in April.</p><p>"I have covered the NFL with professionalism and dedication throughout my career, and I stand behind every story I have ever published. When the Page Six item first appeared, The Athletic supported me unequivocally, expressed confidence in my work and pride in my journalism. For that I am grateful. In the days that followed, unfortunately, commentators in various media have engaged in self-feeding speculation that is simply unmoored from the facts," Russini said then, adding she was stepping away "not because I accept the narrative that has been constructed around this episode, but because I refuse to lend it further oxygen or to let it define me or my career."</p><p>Vrabel said Thursday he didn't have any reaction to the report on Russini, adding he's "moved on" as he prepares for this season.<br></p>
